text: Where an offence involving a breach of contract has been committed, the offender shall be deemed liable for prosecution under the relevant penal provisions, unless the aggrieved party elects to pursue a remedy through civil action alone. In cases where both parties to a contractual dispute consent, and such consent is duly verified by a Magistrate First Class or higher judicial officer, the offence may be compounded as provided herein. The application for compounding shall detail the nature of the breach, the proposed terms of settlement including monetary compensation if applicable, and an acknowledgement of guilt from the offender. Upon satisfaction that the agreement reached is just and equitable to all parties concerned, the Magistrate may pass an order staying further proceedings against the offender. This power to compound offences shall not extend to cases involving fraud or moral turpitude, as determined by the prosecuting authority.

Applications for registration of Gratuity Trusts shall be submitted to the designated Regional Labour Commissioner, along with certified copies of the Trust Deed, a list of Trustees, and details of assets held by the Trust. The Regional Labour Commissioner may, subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act, delegate the power to verify documents and conduct preliminary inquiries relating to such applications to a subordinate officer appointed for that purpose, provided that such delegation is recorded in writing and specifies the extent of authority conferred. Any objection raised against registration shall be communicated to the applicant within thirty days, affording them an opportunity for hearing as prescribed herein. The Regional Labour Commissioner may require additional information or clarification from applicants before making a determination regarding registration.

Applications for registration of Gratuity Trusts shall be submitted to the designated Regional Labour Commissioner in Form A, duly authenticated by the employer and a representative of the employees. The Commissioner may, subject to verification of all details pertaining to the Trust deed, assets held, and beneficiaries identified, register such Trust within thirty days of receipt of application. Where the Commissioner deems it necessary for ensuring proper administration of the Gratuity Trust, he or she may delegate powers relating to inspection and inquiry to a subordinate officer acting under his direction. Such delegation shall be in writing and specify the extent of authority delegated. The employer shall furnish an annual report detailing financial transactions to the Regional Labour Commissioner; failure to do so will invite action as provided herein.

The Central Licensing Authority may, through notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers relating to the grant, renewal, and modification of licenses for processing and distribution of fortified foods to Regional Food Safety Authorities, subject to conditions specified therein. Such delegation shall not extend to the power to revoke a license or impose monetary penalties exceeding one million rupees. Any Regional Food Safety Authority exercising delegated powers under this Act shall submit an annual report detailing all licensing actions taken to the Central Licensing Authority for review. Furthermore, assignment of licenses granted by the Central Licensing Authority is permitted with prior written consent, provided that the assignee undertakes full responsibility for compliance with applicable regulations and standards as provided herein. The Central Licensing Authority may refuse consent to any such assignment if it deems the proposed assignee unsuitable based on their past record concerning food safety practices.

Where an Inquiry Officer appointed under this Act is empowered to examine witnesses and record evidence, such officer shall not delegate their authority to receive testimony or administer oaths except in circumstances where a duly qualified medical professional determines the Inquiry Officer physically incapable of performing these duties. Delegation shall only extend to another person holding a judicial position as defined under the relevant statutes, and must be formally documented with reasons for delegation recorded in writing. The delegated officer shall act subject to the original Inquiry Officer’s direction and oversight. Any evidence obtained through such delegation is admissible provided that the prescribed protocols regarding witness identification and chain of custody are strictly adhered to; failure to comply renders the evidence inadmissible.

Where a judicial officer is legally incapacitated or otherwise unable to perform their duties under this Act, the Chief Justice of the High Court may, by order published in the Official Gazette, delegate specific powers relating to the examination of witnesses and the admission of evidence to another judicial officer deemed suitable. Such delegation shall be for a period not exceeding six months, unless circumstances require an extension, which may only be granted with further notification in the Official Gazette. The delegated officer shall exercise these powers subject to any conditions stipulated by the Chief Justice, including limitations on the types of cases handled and the scope of evidentiary rulings made. Any order of delegation shall specify that it is a temporary measure and does not prejudice the original judicial officer's right to resume their duties upon recovery or reassignment.

Where any establishment employing workmen is required to obtain a licence under this Act for the purpose of granting gratuity to its employees, the conditions of that licence shall be subject to periodic review by the Gratuity Assessment Board. The Board may, after affording the employer an opportunity of being heard and considering representations made, modify or add to such conditions if it is satisfied that the original terms do not adequately ensure compliance with the provisions relating to gratuity calculation and disbursement. Any employer aggrieved by a decision of the Board altering the conditions of their licence may appeal to the Labour Court within thirty days from the date of communication of said decision. The court’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under the relevant appellate jurisdiction as provided herein.

Where a consumer alleges deficiency in service or goods supplied by an operator, the onus of establishing such deficiency shall lie upon the complainant, subject to the provisions regarding presumptions under this Act. Provided that, where the operator fails to produce adequate records substantiating their performance or quality control measures, the Commission may, at its discretion, presume deficiency and proceed accordingly against the operator. Any penalty imposed for failing to adequately substantiate a defense shall be in addition to any compensation awarded to the complainant. The Central Authority may issue directions regarding best practices concerning record-keeping by operators to facilitate fair adjudication under this Act. Operators found wilfully obstructing investigations or suppressing relevant information pertaining to consumer complaints will face enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Where any District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is unable or unwilling to exercise jurisdiction vested in it under this Act, the State Commission may, subject to just cause and after affording the concerned District Forum an opportunity for representation, delegate its powers and functions relating to specific matters to another such Commission within the same State. Such delegation shall be deemed to be without prejudice to the right of appeal as provided herein. Any order passed by a Commission acting under delegated authority is liable to challenge before the appellate forum, and any party aggrieved by an action taken in purported exercise of delegated powers may file a petition seeking quashing of such action, demonstrating that the delegation was unauthorized or exceeded its scope.

Where any District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is satisfied that the nature of the dispute requires specialized expertise not readily available within its existing composition, it may, subject to prior approval from the State Commission, delegate specific adjudicatory powers relating solely to matters of technical assessment to a suitably qualified individual possessing such expertise. Such delegation shall be in writing and clearly define the scope of delegated authority; any order passed by the delegated individual shall be deemed an order of the District Commission for all purposes under this Act. An aggrieved party may appeal from any order, whether original or delegated, to the State Commission within thirty days, challenging both the factual findings and the propriety of the power delegation itself.

Where a food business operator fails to pay any sum due from them under this Act or regulations made thereunder, the State Food Safety Authority may issue a notice requiring payment within thirty days. Failure to comply with such notice shall empower the Authority to recover the outstanding dues as an arrear of land revenue. The amount recoverable shall include principal, interest accruing at the rate specified by the Central Government, and all costs incurred by the Authority in pursuing recovery. Provided that before initiating proceedings for recovery, the Authority shall provide a reasonable opportunity to the food business operator to be heard, including presenting evidence demonstrating inability to pay. Any amounts recovered under this process shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of the State. The Authority may also impose additional penalties as deemed appropriate, subject to principles of natural justice and proportionality.

Where any person has failed to comply with a direction issued under this Act relating to environmental protection or remediation measures, the Central Government shall have the power to recover from that person all costs incurred by the Government in carrying out remedial work necessitated by the failure. Such recovery shall be deemed an arrear of revenue and may be recovered as if it were an arrear of land revenue recoverable under the relevant State enactments. The amount so recoverable shall include, but not be limited to, expenses for site assessment, containment actions, cleanup operations, and monitoring activities undertaken to mitigate environmental damage. Prior to initiating recovery proceedings, notice shall be served upon the defaulting person detailing the nature of the failure, the remedial measures taken, and the sum due. Opportunity of being heard shall be afforded as provided herein.

The power conferred upon an agent by contract to perform certain acts on behalf of the principal may be delegated, provided that such delegation is expressly or impliedly authorized under this Act. Delegation shall not extend to acts which are personal in nature or require a degree of skill or judgment unique to the original agent and specifically contracted for between the principal and the agent. Any act performed by the delegatee within the scope of the permitted delegation shall be binding upon the principal, as if such act were directly undertaken by the agent. The principal remains liable for any acts of the delegatee exceeding the authority expressly or impliedly delegated; however, ratification may discharge this liability as provided herein.

The power conferred upon an agent by contract to perform acts on behalf of the principal may be delegated, subject to the terms of the agreement creating that agency. Delegation is deemed valid unless expressly prohibited within the contractual stipulations or where the nature of the act intrinsically requires the personal skill or diligence of the original agent. An agent shall not delegate powers involving matters of a confidential nature, or which require special trust or discretion, without prior written consent from the principal. Provided that, such delegation does not relieve the original agent from liability for acts performed by the delegatee under this Act.

The Registrar shall receive applications for registration of Gratuity Trusts established by employers subject to this Act. Every such application must include certified copies of the Trust Deed, a list of Trustees with their addresses and occupations, and a declaration confirming compliance with regulations pertaining to gratuity payments. The employer may delegate the responsibility for submitting these documents and attending subsequent inquiries to an authorized representative, provided that written authorization is submitted alongside the initial registration request. Such delegation shall not absolve the employer from ultimate accountability under this Act. Further, the Registrar may require additional documentation or clarifications as deemed necessary to ascertain the Trust's adherence to stipulations outlined herein. The applicant shall be notified of any deficiencies within thirty days of receipt.

Applications for registration of Gratuity Trusts shall be submitted to the Regional Labour Commissioner designated under this Act, along with certified copies of the Trust Deed and a list of Trustees. The Regional Labour Commissioner may delegate his powers relating to scrutiny of applications and verification of documents to such officers as he deems fit, provided that such delegation is recorded in writing and published on the website of the Department. Any objection to the proposed registration shall be communicated to the applicant within thirty days, specifying the grounds for the objection. The applicant shall have a period of fifteen days from the date of receipt of such communication to submit a written response or make necessary modifications to the Trust Deed. Failure to respond may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

Where an inquiry officer appointed under this Act is empowered to examine witnesses and collect evidence, he or she may, subject to prior approval from the appointing authority, delegate such power of examination and collection to a subordinate officer specifically designated for that purpose; provided that such delegation shall only extend to matters directly pertaining to the factual investigation and not to any decision-making functions. The subordinate officer so delegated shall act under the direction and control of the inquiry officer and report all findings promptly. Any evidence collected by a delegate shall be deemed to have been collected by the inquiry officer himself or herself for all purposes under this Act. Further, the appointing authority may prescribe conditions regarding the qualifications and experience required for any such subordinate officer.

Where a judicial officer is legally authorized to exercise powers under this Act, that officer may, subject to the satisfaction of the High Court, delegate those powers in writing to any other judicial officer subordinate to him or her, provided that such delegation specifies the precise nature and extent of the delegated authority. The delegation shall be valid only for a period not exceeding one year unless expressly extended by subsequent order of the High Court. Any action taken by an officer acting under delegated power shall be deemed to have been taken by the delegating judicial officer. Further, no delegation shall extend to powers relating to disciplinary proceedings or matters involving contempt of court. The original judicial officer retains ultimate responsibility for actions undertaken pursuant to a delegation and may revoke it at any time.

Where any District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is satisfied that there exists a compelling reason necessitating the delegation of its powers under this Act to one or more of its presiding officers, it may do so by an order in writing specifying the extent and duration of such delegation. Such order shall be published prominently on the website of the Commission and displayed at its headquarters. Any party directly affected by an action taken pursuant to a delegated power may appeal against that action within thirty days to the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, asserting prejudice arising from the delegation itself. The State Commission shall consider such appeals expeditiously, determining whether the delegation was lawful and appropriately exercised, subject to just cause shown.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules framed thereunder, the Central Authority may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers and functions under Chapter V to any officer or authority subordinate to it, provided that such delegation shall be accompanied by specific guidelines outlining the scope and limitations thereof. Any order passed by an officer acting as delegated agent of the Central Authority is subject to review upon appeal to the said Central Authority within thirty days from the date of communication of the order to the aggrieved party. The Central Authority may entertain appeals notwithstanding any deficiency in adherence to prescribed procedures, but shall consider such deficiencies when determining the merits of the appeal and may direct rectification as deemed necessary.

The power conferred upon an agent by contract to perform certain acts or execute specific instruments on behalf of the principal may be delegated, subject to the terms of the agreement and any express restrictions contained therein. Delegation shall not extend beyond the scope of authority expressly or impliedly granted; an act performed outside such permitted delegation is deemed ultra vires and unenforceable against the principal. The principal remains liable for acts undertaken by a delegatee within the bounds of the delegated power, provided that the delegation was validly made under this Act. Nothing herein shall prevent a principal from revoking any previously conferred delegation at any time, subject to contractual obligations.

The power conferred upon an agent by contract to perform specific acts or manage certain affairs on behalf of the principal may be delegated to another person, provided that such delegation is not expressly prohibited by the terms of the agency agreement. Delegation shall only extend to matters which are incidental to the original authority and do not fundamentally alter the nature of the principal's undertaking. An agent’s right to delegate powers under this Act is subject to the condition that the substituted agent possesses similar or superior competence to perform the delegated functions. The principal retains ultimate responsibility for acts performed by a delegated agent, notwithstanding the delegation.

Where a generating station licence has been granted under this Act, the Central Government may revoke the said licence if it is satisfied that the licensee has failed to comply with the conditions stipulated in the licence, or has made default in payment of any fees payable under this Act, or has otherwise acted in manner prejudicial to the interests of consumers. Such revocation shall not be absolute but shall provide for a period of notice and opportunity to rectify the defaults as provided herein. The licensee shall have the right to make representations against any proposed revocation, which shall be considered by the Central Government before making its final determination. Further, any person aggrieved by an order of revocation may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order; this appeal being a remedy available without prejudice to other rights and remedies under this Act.

Where any gratuity is payable under this Act, but the employer defaults in making payment thereof within thirty days from the date it becomes due, the concerned employee shall have the right to apply for recovery of the said dues through the Labour Commissioner having jurisdiction over the establishment. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the assessment order determining the gratuity amount and any relevant correspondence exchanged between the employer and the employee. Upon receipt of such an application, the Labour Commissioner shall issue notice to the employer requiring it to show cause within fifteen days as to why the dues have not been paid. Failure to comply with this notice or a determination that the employer has failed to pay gratuity shall empower the Labour Commissioner to initiate proceedings for recovery under general principles of law.

Where any gratuity has become due and payable to an employee but remains unpaid at the time of dissolution or closure of the establishment, whether owing to insolvency or otherwise, the employer shall be liable to make recovery of such dues from the estate of the deceased employee, or from any person who inherits the property or effects of the deceased employee. Provided that, where the gratuity is payable to the nominee of the deceased employee, the recovery may be made from the said nominee to the extent of the amount due as gratuity. The employer shall notify such recovery proceedings in writing to the concerned Regional Labour Commissioner and shall furnish all relevant documentation pertaining to the determination of the gratuity liability. Failure to comply with these provisions will render the employer liable for penalties under this Act.

All generating stations, transmission licensees, distribution licensees, and electricity traders shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all activities undertaken under this Act, including but not limited to generation, supply, trading, and wheeling of electrical energy. These records shall be preserved in a manner accessible for inspection by the appropriate authority upon due notice. The maintenance of such records is crucial for ensuring transparency and accountability within the electricity sector. Distribution licensees shall register all consumer connections with unique identification numbers, updating these registrations whenever changes occur to consumer details or load sanctions. All registration alterations must be documented chronologically, alongside relevant supporting documentation submitted at the time of application. Failure to maintain accurate records as provided herein will attract penalties as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Every distribution licensee shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all electricity supplied, including but not limited to meter readings, tariff classifications applied, consumption patterns observed, and any adjustments made under this Act. These records shall be preserved in a durable medium, readily accessible for inspection by authorized officers of the State Commission or relevant government agencies. The licensee may utilize electronic systems for record keeping, provided that such systems ensure data integrity and security as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Failure to maintain adequate records relating to electricity distribution will constitute an offense subject to penalties as determined by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. All entries in registers shall be attested by a duly authorized representative of the licensee. The maintenance of these records is vital for ensuring transparency and accountability within the power sector, as provided herein.

Where an offence has been committed under this Act or regulations made thereunder, the Food Safety and Standards Authority shall have the power to direct compounding of the offence, provided that the offence does not involve a threat to public health or safety, or contravention of any mandatory standard. The authority may, after giving notice to the offender, afford him an opportunity of being heard, consider such representations as he may make, and pass an order directing the offender to pay a monetary penalty within a specified period. Such penalty shall be determined based on the nature and gravity of the offence, and in accordance with guidelines issued by the Central Government. Failure to comply with the compounding order shall render the offender liable for prosecution under this Act as if no such order had been passed. The authority may, at any time, recall a compounding order previously made.

Where an offence has been committed under this Act involving a contravention of regulations prescribing food safety standards or relating to labelling requirements, the Food Safety Officer empowered by the State Food Safety Authority shall serve upon the offender a notice proposing compounding of the said offence. Such notice shall specify the amount proposed to be compounded and the manner in which payment may be made. The offender shall, within seven days from the date of service of such notice, either pay the sum so proposed or submit their written objection to the Food Safety Authority. Upon receipt of an objection, the authority shall afford the offender a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Following due consideration, the authority may confirm, vary, or reject the proposal for compounding of the offence. The amount determined through compounding shall be deposited with the State Government as per rules prescribed by it.

Every establishment required to provide gratuity under this Act shall establish and diligently maintain a Gratuity Register at each place where it employs ten or more employees. The said register shall contain particulars of all employees eligible for gratuity, including their date of joining, designation, last drawn salary, and dates of termination or retirement. Any alteration in an employee’s details shall be recorded promptly with the reason for such modification duly noted. Failure to maintain the Gratuity Register accurately and completely will constitute a violation under this Act. The inspecting officer may require submission of the register for verification at any time, and discrepancies found therein must be rectified immediately. Records pertaining to gratuity payments made shall also be preserved securely for a period not less than seven years.

Every establishment employing twenty or more employees shall establish and maintain a Gratuity Fund Account for each employee eligible under this Act. The said account shall accurately reflect all contributions made by the employer towards gratuity, detailing dates of payment and amounts credited. Failure to adhere to prescribed formats for these records constitutes an offence punishable as provided herein. Where an employee leaves service prior to becoming entitled to gratuity, a summary record indicating the period of service rendered and reasons for cessation of employment shall be preserved. All records pertaining to gratuity entitlements are subject to inspection by designated officers authorized under this Act. The maintenance of accurate and complete records is essential for ensuring compliance with obligations as provided herein.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers and functions under this Act to any officer or authority empowered to exercise similar powers and perform similar functions, provided that such delegation specifies the extent of the delegated power and the conditions subject to which it is exercised. Any authority so delegated shall exercise the powers and discharge the functions delegated to it as if it were the Central Government itself, and shall be bound by all directions and guidelines issued under this Act. The Central Government may also revoke any such delegation at any time, and without assigning any reason.

The Gratuity Authority may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers to perform any function relating to the determination of eligibility for gratuity or the assessment of the amount payable under this Act, to any officer serving within the Authority or to any other Government servant appointed specifically for that purpose. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a clear articulation of the scope and limitations of the delegated authority, specifying the types of cases which may be handled independently and those requiring further review. Any assignment of responsibility relating to the verification of employment records or the investigation of gratuity claims under this Act requires prior written consent from the Gratuity Authority, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. The Authority retains ultimate oversight and may revoke any delegation or assignment at any time, provided that due notice is given to the affected party.

The Central Gratuity Authority may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers to administer gratuity trusts established under this Act to a designated financial institution or other entity approved by the Government. Such delegation shall include the power to accept assignments of gratuity entitlements from employers and to manage the assets held within those trusts. An employer intending to assign their obligations relating to gratuity payments may execute a deed transferring such rights, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein and as provided herein. The Authority shall ensure that any entity receiving such delegation possesses adequate infrastructure and expertise for handling gratuity funds. Further, any assignment of gratuity entitlements is deemed valid only upon registration with the Central Gratuity Authority. This process ensures transparency and accountability in the management of employee benefits.

Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere under this Act, the State Commission may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers relating to the grant of licenses for intra-State transmission and distribution subject to conditions specified therein. Such delegation shall not extend to the power to adjudicate disputes concerning tariff determination or enforcement actions against licensees; however, the Commission may authorize subordinate officers to perform such functions as it deems necessary for efficient administration. Any order passed by an officer acting under delegated authority is liable to be challenged before the State Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of its communication, and any decision of the Tribunal shall be final, subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules framed thereunder, the State Commission may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers relating to the investigation of complaints concerning tariff fixation or license conditions to an officer designated for that purpose. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a clear specification of the extent and duration of the delegated authority. Any order passed by such officer acting under this delegation is subject to review by the State Commission upon appeal filed within sixty days, detailing grounds of prejudice or procedural irregularity. The Commission may affirm, modify, or quash the original order; its decision shall be final. This power of delegation does not extend to matters concerning revocation of licenses or enforcement actions involving criminal penalties under this Act.

Every registered consumer dispute resolution agency shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all complaints received, hearings conducted, orders passed, and recoveries effected under this Act. Such records shall include, but not be limited to, copies of complaint applications, notices issued to parties involved, attendance registers of hearing participants, written arguments submitted, and detailed reasoning supporting each order rendered. The Central Authority may prescribe the form and manner in which these records are maintained, including provisions for electronic storage and retrieval. All agencies shall ensure that such records remain accessible for inspection by authorised officers of the Central Authority or State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions, subject to due process and confidentiality protocols as provided herein. Failure to maintain adequate records, or wilful destruction thereof, shall be deemed a violation under this Act and may attract penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority.

Where any industrial unit engaged in activities listed under Schedule I is required to undertake environmental impact assessment, the unit shall furnish a comprehensive report detailing potential ecological consequences arising from its operations. This report must include, but not be limited to, assessments of air and water quality, noise pollution levels, and waste generation patterns. Failure to provide such a report, or providing a materially inaccurate one, constitutes a violation under this Act and renders the unit liable for penalties as determined by the competent authority. The aggrieved party may challenge any determination regarding the adequacy of disclosure in the prescribed manner before an appellate tribunal; provided that such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of notification of the decision.

Every party to a contract involving the transfer of goods, services, or property shall maintain accurate and complete records pertaining to all transactions undertaken under this Act. Such records shall include, but are not limited to, invoices, receipts, delivery notes, and correspondence relevant to the performance of contractual obligations. Failure to diligently preserve these records for a period of seven years from the date of completion of the contract will constitute a breach, subject to penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. Any person found guilty of obstructing access to or tampering with required records shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, and also to a fine. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines regarding the format and storage of these records, provided that such prescriptions do not unduly burden small businesses.

Every party entering into an agreement involving the transfer of movable property, or providing services requiring ongoing performance, shall maintain complete and accurate records pertaining to all transactions undertaken under this Act. Such records must be preserved for a period not less than seven years from the date of final payment or completion of service, whichever is later. Failure to maintain adequate records, or demonstrable falsification thereof, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, or both. Any officer authorised under this Act may inspect such records; refusal to permit inspection shall be deemed a separate violation subject to penalty. The Central Government may prescribe the form and manner of record keeping as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “gratuity records” includes all documents pertaining to the employment history of an employee, details relating to their salary and wages earned during the period of their service, particulars regarding any leave availed or outstanding, and evidence demonstrating continuous service as required under this Act. The employer shall maintain these gratuity records in a manner that is readily accessible for inspection by designated officers authorized under this Act and by the employees themselves. Failure to adequately preserve such records, or demonstrable negligence in their upkeep, constitutes an offence punishable as provided herein. Further, all entries made within the gratuity records shall be deemed conclusive evidence unless proven otherwise through verifiable documentation.

Where a victim or their legal representative institutes proceedings against an accused relating to an offence involving bodily injury or loss of property, both parties may agree to compound the offence subject to conditions prescribed herein. Such agreement shall be made in writing and attested by at least two independent witnesses who are not related to either party. The Court shall record the terms of the compromise and satisfy itself that it is freely arrived at without coercion or undue influence. Provided that, where the offence involves serious injury as defined under this Act, or loss of property exceeding a specified monetary value, the Court may refuse to accept the agreement for compounding if deemed unjust or disproportionate to the harm suffered. The victim shall be entitled to compensation as determined by the Court even in cases where compounding is permitted.

Where a minor has committed an offence involving theft or mischief, and the owner of the property affected consents to the compounding of the offence, the Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, order that the minor make compensation equivalent to the loss suffered by the complainant. Such compensation shall be paid within a period not exceeding six months from the date of the order. Provided that if the minor fails to comply with the terms of the order regarding payment of compensation, the Court may proceed with the trial as if no such application for compounding had been made. The victim’s consent for compounding shall be recorded in writing before the Court and shall constitute evidence thereof under this Act. This provision does not preclude the Court from considering other factors relevant to the minor's rehabilitation or the severity of the offence.

Every operator of a facility listed in Schedule I shall maintain detailed records pertaining to emissions, effluents, and waste generation, including but not limited to quantities, composition, treatment methods, and disposal locations. Such records shall be preserved for a minimum period of ten years from the date of creation and made available for inspection by authorized officers under this Act. The assignment of responsibility for maintaining these records may occur between entities engaged in joint operation or ownership of the facility, subject to prior written consent from the State Pollution Control Board. Any person acquiring an existing facility shall be bound by the record-keeping obligations previously undertaken by the predecessor operator. Failure to maintain adequate records as provided herein constitutes a violation and is actionable under this Act.

The State Commission shall, upon receiving a request from an appropriate distribution licensee, delegate certain functions relating to tariff determination for low voltage consumers to a committee constituted by the licensee. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a detailed memorandum outlining the specific powers being transferred, including but not limited to approval of consumer connection charges and adjustments to demand surcharges. The Commission may, after giving notice to all stakeholders, revoke any such delegation if it is satisfied that the licensee has failed to adhere to guidelines issued under this Act or has demonstrated an inability to effectively manage the delegated functions. Any officer exercising powers delegated under this Act shall be subject to the directions and oversight of both the distribution licensee and the State Commission. The exercise of delegated powers shall be documented meticulously, with records available for inspection by the Commission upon request.

The Regional Transport Authority shall have power to delegate its functions relating to the grant of permits for transport vehicles under this Act, provided that such delegation shall only extend to subordinate officers specifically designated in writing by the authority. Any officer so delegated shall exercise the powers and discharge the duties assigned to them subject to adherence with prescribed guidelines regarding vehicle type, route allocation, and passenger capacity as detailed in circular notifications issued periodically. The Transport Authority may review any such delegation at intervals not exceeding two years or if circumstances warrant, including instances of non-compliance with regulations or demonstrable operational inefficiencies. Further, no power relating to the revocation of a permit shall be delegated under this Act.

The Regional Transport Authority shall have power to delegate its functions relating to the grant of permits for transport vehicles under this Act to an officer designated by it, provided that such delegation is recorded in writing and specifies the extent of powers delegated. Any order passed by an officer acting with delegated authority shall be deemed to have been passed by the Regional Transport Authority itself. The delegation may be revoked or modified at any time by a written order specifying the reasons for such revocation or modification. No such delegation shall extend to matters concerning appeals under this Act, nor to decisions relating to the suspension or cancellation of permits. An officer exercising delegated powers shall comply with all applicable procedures and guidelines as provided herein.

For the purposes of ensuring accountability and facilitating effective environmental management, all authorities empowered to grant approvals or undertake activities affecting the environment shall maintain comprehensive records relating thereto. These records shall include, but are not limited to, applications received, assessments conducted, decisions taken, conditions imposed, and monitoring data collected under this Act. The maintenance of such records shall be in a form accessible for public scrutiny, subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein concerning confidential commercial information or matters pertaining to national security. Failure to maintain adequate records may render the responsible officer liable to penalties as prescribed.

For the purposes of ensuring accountability and facilitating effective environmental management, every authority empowered to grant approvals or issue consents under this Act shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all applications received, assessments conducted, and decisions rendered. These records shall include, but are not limited to, details regarding project proponents, proposed activities, potential environmental impacts, mitigation measures implemented, and compliance monitoring reports. The maintenance of such records is mandatory and subject to periodic audits as provided herein. Any information contained within these records shall be accessible to the public, subject to reasonable restrictions protecting confidential commercial data.

Where a motor vehicle owner or driver commits an offence which is compoundable under this Act, the concerned Transport Officer or such officer authorised by the State Government in this behalf may, at his discretion, entertain an application from the offender seeking compounding of the said offence. Such application shall be accompanied by a sum determined by the officer, representing the penalty for the infraction and costs associated with administrative processing. The officer shall provide notice to any individual demonstrably prejudiced by the offence, affording them an opportunity to object to the proposed compounding. If no objection is received within thirty days or if all objections are overruled, the Transport Officer may order the compounding of the offence upon payment of the prescribed sum. This process does not preclude further action under this Act where the nature of the offence warrants it.

Where a food business operator is found to have committed an offence involving substandard quality or misbranding of food, the Food Safety Officer may, subject to certain conditions, initiate proceedings for compounding of such offences. This power shall be exercised only where the contravention does not pertain to matters affecting public health and safety. The concerned officer shall issue a notice specifying the nature of the alleged offence and the amount proposed for compounding, provided that the amount determined shall not exceed the penalty prescribed under this Act. Any food business operator aggrieved by such notice may elect to appear before the adjudicating officer and contest the charges. If the offender chooses to accept the compounding offer, they shall pay the stipulated sum within a specified period; failure to do so will result in further legal action as provided herein.

Where a food business operator is found to have committed an offence involving substandard quality or misbranding of food, the Food Safety Officer may, subject to certain conditions, initiate proceedings for compounding of such offences. This power shall be exercised only where the contravention does not pertain to matters affecting public health and safety, nor involve persistent violations under this Act. The prescribed fee for compounding shall be determined based on the nature and severity of the offence, as notified by the Central Government from time to time. Provided that any food business operator desiring to avail of the option of compounding must apply in writing within thirty days of receiving notice of the alleged contravention. Failure to comply with this provision will preclude them from seeking such remedy. The decision regarding compounding is subject to judicial review.

The rights to recover dues arising from contracts settled through arbitration proceedings under this Act are assignable subject to the terms of the original contract and any subsequent agreement between the parties. Provided that, where a party has obtained an arbitral award relating to such recovery, the assignment of the right to enforce said award shall require prior written consent of the other contracting party. Such consent may be withheld only for demonstrable cause related to the assignor’s financial stability or potential prejudice to the assignee's ability to perform obligations under the original contract. Further, any sub-assignment of a right to recover dues is permissible with the express authorization contained within the initial assignment agreement. The arbitration tribunal shall have the power to determine whether an assignment has been effected in compliance with these provisions and may grant appropriate remedies if violations are found.

The Regional Transport Authority shall have the power to delegate functions relating to the issuance of permits for transport vehicles, including but not limited to assessing applications, conducting inspections, and determining suitability based on prescribed criteria. Such delegation may extend to any officer appointed by the authority specifically for this purpose, provided that the delegated officer possesses qualifications as determined by the authority. The Regional Transport Authority shall issue a formal notification detailing the scope of powers delegated and the duration of such delegation. Any decision taken by an officer acting under delegated authority is deemed to be taken on behalf of the Regional Transport Authority itself. Further, any appeal against an order passed by a delegated officer may be made directly to the Regional Transport Authority, bypassing intermediate appellate bodies as provided herein. The authority may revoke or modify any delegation at any time and without assigning reasons.

Every Regional Transport Authority shall have power to delegate to an Authorised Officer appointed by the State Government, specific functions relating to the issuance of permits for transport vehicles, including but not limited to verification of documents submitted under this Act and assessment of fitness certificates. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a written instrument detailing the precise powers conferred and any limitations imposed upon the Authorised Officer’s exercise thereof. The Regional Transport Authority may revoke such delegation at any time, providing fifteen days' notice in writing to the Authorised Officer. No act or omission undertaken by an Authorised Officer acting within the scope of delegated authority shall render the Regional Transport Authority liable. Any appeal against a decision made by an Authorised Officer exercising delegated powers shall be directly addressed to the Regional Transport Authority for review and determination, as provided herein.

Where a local authority or any other agency entrusted with environmental protection functions fails to remit sums due to the Central Government under this Act towards costs incurred for remediation of polluted sites, or for undertaking measures mandated by directions issued under section 19, the Central Government shall issue a notice requiring remittance within sixty days. Failure to comply with such notice shall render the defaulting authority liable to pay interest at the rate of twelve percent per annum on the outstanding amount from the date the sum became due. The Central Government may, subject to conditions as provided herein, recover these dues through attachment of assets or other means deemed appropriate. Any dispute concerning the assessment of costs or validity of recovery shall be resolved by a Tribunal established under this Act.

Where an offence under this Act relates to a violation of rules regarding vehicle dimensions or load limits, the Motor Vehicles Department may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, permit compounding of the said offence. Such compounding shall only be permissible if the offender presents themselves before the designated officer within fourteen days of the date of issue of the memorandum of offence and pays a sum equivalent to fifty percent of the penalty that would otherwise be imposed under this Act. Provided that, where the vehicle involved is used for commercial purposes, compounding shall not be allowed unless satisfactory proof of valid insurance coverage is presented at the time of application. The officer may refuse compounding if satisfied that the violation posed a significant risk to public safety or resulted in damage to property.

Where an offence under this Act is committed involving a motor vehicle, the offender shall, subject to compliance with the provisions outlined below, be afforded the opportunity for compounding of the said offence. Compounding shall only occur where the offence does not involve injury or loss of life and the jurisdictional Magistrate deems it appropriate after considering the nature of the violation and the record of the offender. Provided that, if the offender fails to appear before the Court on the date fixed, or demonstrates a lack of genuine intent towards rectifying the transgression, compounding shall be denied. The amount for compounding may be determined by the Magistrate, not exceeding an amount equivalent to twice the penalty prescribed under this Act for such offence and shall be paid within thirty days.

Where a Public Information Officer is unable or unwilling to exercise powers vested in them under this Act, they may, subject to approval from the designated Appellate Authority within their respective public authority, delegate such powers to another officer deemed suitable by the appointing authority. Such delegation shall be recorded in writing and made available for public inspection, indicating the specific functions transferred and the period of validity of the delegation. Any action taken by an officer acting as a delegatee shall be binding on the Public Information Officer who authorized the delegation. A citizen aggrieved by any decision or inaction resulting from such delegated power may file an appeal before the Appellate Authority, notwithstanding that the authority was involved in the initial delegation process. The public authority shall ensure accountability for decisions made under delegated powers and provide redressal mechanisms as provided herein.

Where a Public Information Officer is unable or unwilling to exercise powers vested in them under this Act due to exigencies of service or unforeseen circumstances, they may delegate such powers to an appropriately designated officer within the same public authority, provided that such delegation is recorded in writing and made available for public inspection. The delegating officer shall remain ultimately responsible for ensuring compliance with obligations imposed by this Act. Any citizen demonstrating prejudice arising from a decision taken pursuant to delegated power may appeal directly to the original Public Information Officer or their superior designated under Section 8(1)(b), irrespective of whether the delegation was formally recorded. Failure to adequately supervise delegated functions, resulting in demonstrable denial of information rights, shall constitute an act of maladministration subject to disciplinary action as provided herein.

Every business entity engaged in providing goods or services to consumers shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to consumer transactions, complaints received, resolutions offered, and any subsequent disputes arising therefrom. Such records shall be preserved electronically or in physical form, as determined by the Central Authority, for a minimum period of five years from the date of the relevant transaction. Failure to adequately maintain these records constitutes an offence under this Act and is subject to a penalty not exceeding two lakh rupees. The business entity shall also provide access to such records upon request by the Central Authority or any authorized officer acting in accordance with procedures as provided herein. Any attempt to tamper with, destroy, or conceal relevant data will attract enhanced penalties, including potential revocation of licenses.

Every business engaged in providing goods or services to consumers shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to consumer transactions, complaints received, resolutions offered, and any subsequent disputes arising therefrom. These records must be preserved electronically or in physical form, as determined by the Central Authority, for a minimum period of five years from the date of the transaction. Failure to adequately maintain such records, or demonstrable evidence of tampering with said records, shall constitute an offence under this Act. The relevant adjudicating officer may impose a penalty not exceeding two lakh rupees and issue directions for corrective action. Repeated offences may result in suspension of business license as provided herein.

Where a Central Authority deems it necessary to ensure effective enforcement of consumer rights under this Act, it may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers relating to investigation, assessment of compensation, and imposition of penalties to any officer designated specifically for that purpose. Such delegation shall be accompanied by clear guidelines specifying the limits of authority conferred and the procedures to be followed during investigations. Any officer exercising delegated powers shall submit regular reports detailing actions taken and penalties imposed, subject to review by the Central Authority. Failure to comply with prescribed procedural safeguards or exceeding delegated powers will render such officer liable for disciplinary action under applicable service rules, and may result in recovery of any improperly levied penalty from that officer's salary.

Any Central Authority established under this Act may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers to any officer subordinate to it, subject to such conditions as it deems fit. Such delegation shall not extend to the power of imposing penalties or initiating investigations relating to unfair trade practices. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by an officer acting with delegated authority may appeal to the Central Authority within thirty days of receipt of that order. Failure to comply with any direction issued under this Act, or obstruction of any investigation undertaken pursuant to a delegation, shall be deemed a cognizable offence and is subject to penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.

Service of notices issued under this Act shall be effected in the manner prescribed by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. Such notifications shall specify the modes of service including but not limited to registered post with acknowledgment due, courier services authorized by the Board, and personal delivery. The competent authority may determine that for certain categories of notices relating to imminent environmental hazards, immediate communication via electronic mail is permissible as an additional mode of service, provided that proof of transmission is maintained in a secure digital format. Any person served notice shall be deemed to have received it on the date indicated on such proof of delivery or transmission. Failure to effect service through the prescribed manner shall not invalidate the contents of the notice unless demonstrable prejudice results from said failure. The Central Government may, by general order, prescribe alternative methods for ensuring effective communication under this Act.

Any arbitration agreement lawfully entered into under this Act shall remain valid notwithstanding any subsequent modification of the powers delegated to an arbitrator by the parties or by law. Where an authority empowered to appoint arbitrators delegates its functions relating to appointment, subject to prior written consent from the High Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the dispute arises, such delegation shall not invalidate appointments made pursuant thereto. Any person failing to comply with a direction issued under this Act concerning the validity of delegated powers shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty as determined by the presiding officer, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Repeated or willful non-compliance may result in further penalties and potential disqualification from serving as an arbitrator.

Where an arbitral award has been enforced under this Act, and proceedings are initiated to challenge the validity of such enforcement based on allegations of fraud or misrepresentation relating to the arbitration agreement itself, the Court shall admit such challenge notwithstanding that the limitation period for challenging the underlying arbitral award may have expired. Provided that the party seeking to challenge the enforcement demonstrates with reasonable certainty a substantial risk of material prejudice resulting from the alleged fraud or misrepresentation. Failure to demonstrate said risk within ninety days of the order enforcing the award will preclude further proceedings under this provision and render any subsequent attempts at challenging the enforcement void ab initio. The Court may, subject to just considerations, impose costs reflective of frivolous applications made in bad faith.

The Regional Transport Authority shall have power to delegate its functions relating to the grant of permits for transport vehicles under this Act to any officer designated by it in writing; provided that such delegation shall not extend to the consideration of appeals against decisions regarding permit rejection or cancellation, nor to matters concerning the determination of fares exceeding established limits. Any decision taken by an officer acting as a delegate is subject to review and reversal by the Regional Transport Authority upon written application demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from any error of law or fact. The authority may entertain such applications within ninety days of the delegated officer’s original order, and its decision on such review shall be final, notwithstanding any provision regarding judicial remedy under this Act.

The Regional Transport Authority may, subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, delegate its powers relating to the grant of permits for transport vehicles to any officer designated by the State Government; provided that such delegation shall be exercised only with respect to applications received prior to the date specified in the notification issued by the government. Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an officer acting under this delegated authority may appeal to the Regional Transport Authority within thirty days of receipt of the order, and the authority shall consider the appeal de novo. The power to delegate functions as provided herein does not extend to matters concerning the revocation of permits or imposition of penalties under this Act, which remain exclusively with the Regional Transport Authority for final adjudication.

Where a Public Information Officer is unable or unavailable to perform their duties due to exigencies of service or other unavoidable circumstances, the designated First Appellate Authority shall have the power to temporarily delegate those powers to another officer within the same public authority. Such delegation shall be in writing and specify the period for which the delegated officer will exercise the functions of the Public Information Officer. The original Public Information Officer shall resume their duties upon cessation of the circumstances necessitating the delegation, as determined by the First Appellate Authority. Any order passed by the delegated officer shall be deemed to have been passed by the First Appellate Authority itself and is subject to appeal under this Act. No such delegation shall extend beyond a period of thirty days without further authorization from the Information Commission. The authority exercising delegated powers must adhere strictly to the procedures outlined herein.

Registration of Demand Notices relating to Goods and Services. Every seller providing goods or services is required to maintain a register for recording all notices of demand received from consumers regarding defects in those goods or deficiencies in those services. Such registers shall be preserved securely, both in physical and electronic form, for a period not less than three years from the date of the relevant transaction. Any alteration made to an entry in the register must be authenticated by the seller’s authorized representative with clear indication of the date and reason for such modification. The Central Authority may prescribe guidelines regarding the format and content of these registers, ensuring uniformity across all sellers. Failure to maintain or provide access to this register upon request from a consumer forum constitutes a violation under this Act.

Where a license to operate as a Consumer Dispute Resolution Agency has been granted under this Act, the licensee may assign or otherwise transfer all rights and obligations pertaining to said license to another entity subject to prior approval from the Central Authority. Such approval shall not be withheld arbitrarily and reasons for denial must be recorded in writing and communicated to the applicant within thirty days. The Central Authority may impose conditions on any such assignment ensuring continued compliance with standards of consumer service as provided herein. Further, a licensee seeking revocation of an assigned license shall provide written notice to both the assignee and the Central Authority at least ninety days prior to the intended date of revocation. Grounds for revocation in this instance include demonstrable failure by the assignee to adhere to licensing conditions or persistent complaints regarding unfair dispute resolution practices.

A license granted to a franchisee under this Act relating to the supply of goods or provision of services shall remain valid subject to adherence to the terms stipulated therein; however, the licensor may revoke such license upon written notice to the licensee if material breaches occur concerning quality standards as defined by regulations framed thereunder. Assignment of franchise rights, including intellectual property associated therewith, is permissible with prior consent from the Central Authority, provided that the assignee undertakes all obligations and liabilities incumbent on the original franchisee. The grounds for revocation extend to instances where the franchisee engages in unfair trade practices or misrepresents goods or services, thereby jeopardizing consumer interests as protected under this Act. Further, a license may be revoked if the licensee consistently fails to meet performance benchmarks established by the licensor, subject to due process and opportunity for redressal.

Where a judicial officer is entrusted with the responsibility of determining evidentiary matters relating to claims arising from contractual obligations, such officer may, subject to due process and principles of natural justice, delegate specific powers pertaining to the examination of witnesses or the assessment of documentary evidence to an appropriately qualified legal professional appointed by the court. Such delegation shall be recorded in writing and clearly define the scope of authority conferred. Any party aggrieved by a decision rendered under delegated power may appeal directly to the presiding judicial officer within thirty days of such decision, demonstrating prejudice arising from the delegation itself or errors committed during the exercise of that delegated authority. The right to challenge the validity of the delegation is explicitly preserved, provided it is raised contemporaneously with the substantive challenge to the finding. This provision shall not preclude a judicial officer from seeking assistance and guidance from external experts.

Where a judicial officer is temporarily absent or unable to perform their duties, the High Court may, by order published in the Official Gazette, delegate such powers as are necessary for the efficient administration of justice within that jurisdiction to another judicial officer deemed fit by the court. Such delegation shall be subject to conditions specified in the order and may include limitations on the types of cases or matters which the delegated officer can adjudicate. Any decision rendered by an officer acting under this delegation shall have the same force and effect as if it were made by the original judicial officer. A person aggrieved by a decision taken pursuant to such delegation may appeal directly to the High Court, notwithstanding any provision under this Act relating to appeals from subordinate courts. The power of delegation conferred herein does not extend to matters involving contempt of court or disciplinary proceedings against other judicial officers.

Where a distribution licensee fails to pay any amount due from it to a generating company or transmission licensee within sixty days of the date on which such payment becomes due, the concerned State Electricity Regulatory Commission may direct the distribution licensee to recover the outstanding dues, together with interest at a rate not exceeding twelve per cent per annum, from the consumers. Such recovery shall be proportionate to the quantum of electricity consumed by each consumer and reflected in their subsequent bills. The Commission shall provide an opportunity for the distribution licensee to make representations before issuing such direction. Provided that, if the delay in payment is attributable to circumstances beyond the control of the distribution licensee, as certified by the State Government, the Commission may waive or modify the recovery mechanism under this Act.

The Authority granting a licence under this Act shall not impose conditions that are arbitrary or unreasonable, provided that such conditions are demonstrably necessary to ensure compliance with environmental regulations pertaining to the extraction of mineral resources. Every licensee shall adhere strictly to the approved mining plan and any subsequent modifications thereto, as determined by the competent geological survey authority. Failure to do so may result in suspension or revocation of the licence. The Authority is empowered to conduct periodic inspections to verify adherence to these conditions and to assess the impact on local communities. Any deviation from prescribed extraction methods requires prior written approval from the Authority, subject to a public hearing process as provided herein.

Where any dispute arises concerning the reasonableness or necessity of an entry undertaken under this Act by an authorized officer for the purpose of ascertaining whether gratuity has been paid in accordance with its provisions, either the employer or the employee may appeal to the Labour Court having jurisdiction over the matter. Such appeal shall be made within thirty days from the date the aggrieved party becomes aware of the action taken. The Labour Court shall consider any evidence presented by both parties and determine whether the entry was justified under the circumstances. Provided that an entry deemed unlawful by the Labour Court may be re-instituted only upon obtaining prior written consent from the affected employee, subject to further review as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “gratuity” means the payment in cash of a sum calculated on the basis of the last drawn salary and length of service, subject to the conditions specified herein; "last drawn salary" includes all allowances forming an integral part of emoluments; "length of service" shall be determined as continuous service rendered by an employee; “employee” with reference to establishments governed by this Act means any person employed for wages, whether in a managerial or supervisory capacity or in manual work; and the period within which legal proceedings may be instituted under this Act is limited to three years from the date gratuity becomes payable, notwithstanding any injunction or order restraining such institution, and such limitation operates as a bar to all actions not brought within that period of limitation.

Where gratuity remains unpaid due to the insolvency or liquidation of an establishment, the Controlling Authority shall have power to direct the recovery of such dues from the assets of the establishment available for distribution to creditors. Such direction shall be issued after affording the employer, its legal representatives, and any other interested party a reasonable opportunity of being heard under this Act. The amount recoverable shall include gratuity payable to employees along with interest thereon at the rate specified by the Central Government. Any dispute regarding the determination of eligibility or quantum of gratuity shall be determined by the Controlling Authority in accordance with procedures established herein. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe a time limit within which claims for recovery of unpaid gratuity must be made. Failure to comply with such prescribed timelines shall ordinarily preclude the claim, subject to just cause being demonstrated.

Where an offence involving a breach of contract or other civil wrong has been committed, the offender shall be deemed capable of compounding the offence with the injured party, subject to the satisfaction of the Presiding Officer. The application for compounding shall be made in Form A and accompanied by an affidavit verifying the terms proposed for such composition. Upon receipt of the application, the Presiding Officer may direct both parties to appear before him or her at a mutually convenient time and place. The offender’s proposal concerning compensation or restitution must specify the amount and manner of payment, as well as any other conditions agreed upon. Provided that the injured party consents in writing to the proposed compounding, and the Presiding Officer is satisfied that the terms are just and equitable, an order for compounding may be passed. Any subsequent default in complying with the terms of such order shall render it unenforceable.

Where an employer fails to pay gratuity within thirty days from the date it becomes payable under this Act, the Controlling Authority shall issue notice requiring the employer to remit the arrears of gratuity together with interest at the rate of twelve per centum per annum from the date the gratuity became due until actual payment. Failure to comply with such notice shall render the employer liable to pay a penalty equivalent to fifteen percentum of the outstanding gratuity amount, recoverable as civil debt. The Authority may further direct the recovery of costs incurred in pursuing this action. Any sum recovered under this provision shall be deemed to be gratuity payable and distributed accordingly, subject to any order made by the Labour Court.

For the purposes of this Act, “compoundable offence” means an offence which is declared by law to be compoundable; it being understood that offences against honour, modesty and personal dignity, as determined by notification issued by the Central Government, shall invariably be deemed non-compoundable. An offence may be compounded under this Act only if both the complainant and the accused consent to such compounding, provided that such consent is recorded in writing before a Magistrate. The acceptance of such composition shall extinguish any liability for future prosecution relating to the said offence; however, it does not preclude proceedings taken against an individual for any other offence arising out of the same transaction.

Where an offence involving bodily injury or loss of property is compounded by the parties by agreement in manner provided herein, the offender shall be deemed to have discharged the punishment he would but for such compounding have suffered under this Act. For the purposes of this section, “compounding” means a settlement reached between the offender and the victim, or their respective legal representatives, whereby the offender undertakes to make restitution or provide compensation as agreed upon. Such agreement shall be in writing and verified before an authority authorized by law. The acceptance of such composition does not preclude further proceedings under any other law for the same act unless specifically barred.

Registration of Arbitration Agreements Containing Disclosure Obligations Where an arbitration agreement is executed pursuant to a contract for construction or engineering works, or relating to intellectual property rights, the parties shall be deemed to have implicitly acknowledged their respective duties of disclosure under this Act. Such agreements, prior to becoming enforceable, must be registered with the designated jurisdictional authority within thirty days of execution. The registration form shall include a sworn declaration by each party affirming full and accurate disclosure of all material facts relevant to the subject matter of the arbitration agreement. Failure to provide such a declaration, or subsequent discovery of non-disclosure impacting the fairness of proceedings, may render the entire agreement voidable at the discretion of the arbitral tribunal, as provided herein. The authority shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing registered agreements and any associated declarations.

Any contract entered into in pursuance of an offer that has been communicated to the promisor, and which remains revocable until acceptance, shall remain valid notwithstanding subsequent revocation by the offeror, subject to penalties as prescribed herein. Where revocation is effected through a means different from that employed in the initial communication of the offer, or where such revocation is demonstrably misleading, the offeror shall be liable for damages sustained by the offeree reasonably relying on the continued validity of the contract. The amount of compensation recoverable shall not exceed twice the value of the benefit conferred upon the offeror prior to notification of revocation. Failure to provide timely notice of revocation constitutes a breach under this Act and attracts proportionate financial penalties, as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority.

Where an Arbitral Tribunal is constituted with three arbitrators, the presiding arbitrator shall possess the authority to delegate specific procedural functions relating to case management, document submission, and scheduling of hearings to a designated officer appointed by the arbitration institution administering the proceedings, provided that such delegation does not extend to decisions concerning substantive issues of law or fact. The presiding arbitrator shall provide written notification to all parties regarding any such delegation, detailing the scope and limitations thereof. Any party may object to the delegation within fourteen days from receipt of the notification, after which the Arbitral Tribunal shall review the objection and determine its validity; a decision on this matter is final. This power of delegation under this Act shall not permit the transfer of responsibility for ensuring impartiality or confidentiality of proceedings.

Where an Arbitral Tribunal is constituted with three arbitrators, the presiding arbitrator shall possess the authority to delegate specific procedural functions relating to case management, including but not limited to scheduling hearings, setting deadlines for submission of documents, and issuing directions regarding the conduct of proceedings, to any one of the other two arbitrators. Such delegation shall be documented in writing and made available to all parties involved in the arbitration. The presiding arbitrator may also delegate authority related to administrative tasks necessary for the efficient operation of the Tribunal, provided that such delegation does not extend to decisions concerning substantive issues of law or fact. Any party aggrieved by a decision taken under delegated power may challenge its validity before the presiding arbitrator, who shall review the matter and issue an order. The exercise of delegated powers is subject to the principles of fairness and natural justice as provided herein.

Every food business operator shall maintain detailed records relating to all aspects of their operations, including but not limited to raw material procurement, manufacturing processes, packaging procedures, storage conditions, distribution channels, and sales transactions. These records must be preserved for a minimum period of six years from the date of such transaction or activity, whichever is later, and made available for inspection by authorised officers upon request. The format of these records may be either physical or electronic, provided that electronic records are secured against tampering and loss, and readily accessible. Failure to maintain adequate records shall constitute an offence under this Act. Any officer inspecting the premises may require production of such records and may examine them in detail. The food business operator is obliged to provide all necessary assistance for verification purposes. Records pertaining to allergens present in any food product must be prominently displayed as provided herein.

Every food business operator engaged in manufacture, processing, packing, storage or wholesale of any article of food shall maintain records relating to the procurement of raw materials, production and disposal of finished goods, quality control measures implemented, and details of personnel handling food. These records shall be preserved for a minimum period as may be prescribed under this Act and made available for inspection by authorized officers upon request.
