The term "records" includes, but is not limited to, ledgers, invoices, stock registers, temperature logs, and any other documentation pertinent to the traceability of food products. Failure to maintain such records shall constitute an offence subject to penalty as provided herein.

For the purposes of ensuring traceability and accountability in relation to food safety, every manufacturer, importer, distributor, retailer, or vendor shall maintain records relating to their activities concerning any article of food handled by them. Such records shall include details regarding procurement, production, processing, packaging, storage, transportation, sale, and distribution of such articles. The term "records" includes, but is not limited to, invoices, receipts, stock registers, temperature logs, delivery notes, and batch numbers. Maintenance of these records shall be for a period as may be prescribed under this Act. These records are subject to inspection by authorized officers; provided that the format and content of such records may be specified through regulations.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe a scheme for the assignment of claims arising from liabilities incurred under this Act relating to motor vehicles involved in accidents resulting in injury or death. Such scheme shall provide that any insurance company holding a valid policy covering a vehicle liable for such damages may assign its right to recover dues from the defaulting party to another entity, including but not limited to collection agencies and financial institutions, subject to prior approval of the Transport Authority. The assignment shall include all rights, title, and interest in respect of outstanding claims, along with supporting documentation as deemed necessary by the Transport Authority. Any such assignment is valid only if it adheres to guidelines issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. Further, the original insurer remains liable for ensuring compliance with consumer protection provisions under this Act even after assignment.

Where an offence has been committed under this Act or in contravention of any direction issued under it, the Central Government or any officer authorized by it in this behalf may direct the offender to pay a sum of money as compounding amount. The compounding amount shall be determined based on the nature and gravity of the offence, the extent of environmental damage caused, and the economic conditions of the offender. Provided that such direction for compounding shall only be issued where the ambient air quality standards or water quality standards have not been demonstrably exceeded beyond permissible limits. No compounding shall be ordered in cases involving willful negligence or repeated violations as provided herein.

Where an arbitration agreement is challenged under this Act on the ground that it is invalid or unenforceable, a party seeking to restrain enforcement of the agreement shall institute proceedings within a period of two years from the date when the arbitral award was sought to be enforced, or where no such award exists, from the date when the dispute first arose. Provided that, if the challenge relates to the validity of the arbitration agreement itself and not merely its enforceability in relation to a particular claim, the said limitation period shall commence from the date on which the party seeking to restrain enforcement became aware of the grounds for challenging the agreement's validity. The provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein are subject to any applicable statutory modification or judicial interpretation concerning equitable considerations where demonstrable prejudice results from strict adherence thereto.

Registration of powers delegated under contracts shall be mandatory for all agreements exceeding a value of fifty thousand rupees involving the transfer of operational responsibilities. Such delegation must explicitly identify the original contracting party and the delegatee, detailing the specific functions and authorities conferred. The instrument of delegation shall be executed in the presence of at least two witnesses attesting to its authenticity. Failure to register a delegated power renders the actions undertaken by the delegatee voidable at the option of the original contracting party. Any modification or revocation of such delegation requires subsequent registration, mirroring the initial process as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all registered delegations, accessible for inspection subject to applicable privacy regulations.

Where a registered society, constituted under this Act, desires to delegate its powers relating to the management of immovable property vested in it, it shall submit an instrument of delegation to the Registrar for registration. Such instrument shall clearly define the extent and nature of the delegated authority, specifying the individuals or committees empowered to act on behalf of the society concerning such property. The delegation shall be valid only upon registration by the Registrar, subject to a fee as prescribed. Any transfer of immovable property undertaken pursuant to an unregistered delegation shall be deemed void. Further, no power relating to alteration of bye-laws or amendment of the memorandum shall be delegated under this Act. The instrument of delegation may be revoked by resolution passed at a general body meeting and reported to the Registrar for record.

Where a food business operator manufactures, processes, packs, or imports any packaged commodity intended for sale, they shall prominently display upon such packaging, in clear and legible lettering, all ingredients used therein, arranged in descending order by weight. Failure to comply with this provision constitutes a violation under this Act. Any consumer demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the omission or misrepresentation of an ingredient listed as required herein may initiate proceedings before the appropriate adjudicating officer. Such proceedings shall be subject to appeal to the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of the order being passed by the adjudicating officer, provided that the appellant demonstrates a prima facie case of material non-disclosure and resultant harm. The burden of proving such prejudice rests upon the complainant.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to maintain records in a manner that facilitates access to information as required under this Act, or where such failure demonstrably impedes the exercise of the right to information by a citizen, the Central Information Commission may, after affording the officer an opportunity for being heard, direct the officer to rectify the deficiencies within a specified period. Further, the Commission shall impose a penalty on the Public Information Officer, recoverable from their salary, not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees for each instance of such failure. Any person claiming redress for denial of information due to inadequate record keeping may file a complaint before the Central Information Commission; provided that the complainant has first exhausted available remedies under this Act. The Commission shall consider such complaints and pass appropriate orders as deemed just.

Where any offence has been committed under this Act or regulations framed thereunder, the State Electricity Regulatory Commission may, subject to conditions specified herein, entertain an application from the offender for compounding of the said offence. Provided that no such application shall be entertained in cases involving theft of electricity or tampering with meters, unless the offender demonstrates satisfactory evidence of rehabilitation and restitution to the affected distribution licensee. The Commission shall provide notice to the aggrieved distribution licensee and any other relevant stakeholder before considering a proposal for compounding, affording them an opportunity to submit objections which shall be duly considered. Any order made by the Commission regarding compounding may be appealed against within sixty days to the appellate tribunal, as provided herein.

Where a gratuity is withheld from an eligible employee due to misrepresentation or fraudulent concealment of facts by the employee relating to their employment, the Controlling Authority may, upon receiving a written application from the employer accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating such misrepresentation or concealment, direct the employer to compound the offence. Such direction shall be subject to the condition that the employee was unaware of the true nature of the circumstances at the time of joining service and that the amount of gratuity withheld does not exceed twice the calculated gratuity under this Act. The Authority may also require the employee to repay any benefits already received, as deemed appropriate. This power of compounding shall be exercised only after affording the employee a reasonable opportunity for hearing and representation, ensuring fairness in the determination of redressal.

Every party entering into a contract for the provision of goods or services exceeding a value of one hundred thousand rupees shall establish and diligently maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all transactions undertaken under that agreement. Such records shall include, but are not limited to, invoices, receipts, delivery notes, correspondence relating to payment terms, and any amendments made to the original contractual obligations. The obligation to maintain these records shall continue for a period of seven years from the date of completion of the contract or until all disputes arising therefrom have been resolved, whichever is later. Failure to comply with this provision may render the defaulting party liable to penalties as provided herein and subject to audit by an officer authorized under this Act. The prescribed format for record keeping shall be determined by the relevant government authority.

Every party entering into a contract for the provision of goods or services exceeding a value of one hundred thousand rupees shall establish and diligently maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all transactions undertaken under that agreement. Such records shall include, but are not limited to, details of parties involved, dates of performance, descriptions of goods or services rendered, amounts transacted, and any adjustments made as per the contractual terms. Failure to maintain these records in a manner readily accessible for inspection by authorized officers shall constitute a breach of contract, subject to remedies available under this Act. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines regarding the format and duration for which such records must be preserved. Provided that, digital records maintained in accordance with established security protocols shall have the same evidentiary value as physical documents.

For the purposes of this Act, “outstanding dues” means any sum due from a food vendor or importer to the Central Government or State Food Safety Authority arising from penalties imposed under this Act, fees levied for licenses and registrations, or costs incurred in seizing unsafe food as provided herein. Outstanding dues shall include interest accrued thereon at a rate determined by notification of the Central Government. Recovery of these outstanding dues may be initiated through civil courts having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to any limitations prescribed regarding recovery from agricultural income. The Authority shall provide notice to the debtor prior to initiating recovery proceedings and may accept a repayment plan as deemed appropriate.

For the purposes of this Act, “Dues” means any sum owed to the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India or State Food Safety Authorities arising from penalties imposed under this Act, fees levied for services rendered, or reimbursements claimed for expenses incurred in carrying out functions as provided herein. Dues shall include interest accrued at a rate determined by notification issued by the Central Government. The term “Recovery” signifies the process whereby such Dues are obtained through legal mechanisms available to the Authority, subject to limitations prescribed under general principles of law regarding recovery of government dues. Recovery may be initiated against any person or entity liable for the Dues.

Applications for registration of Eco-Sensitive Zones, as provided herein, shall be submitted to the State Level Appraisal Committee in triplicate, along with a detailed Environmental Impact Assessment report and a comprehensive biodiversity survey conducted by an accredited institution. The Central Government may, through notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers relating to the verification of these reports and the subsequent registration process to designated officers within the Ministry or to such other authorities as it deems appropriate. Such delegation shall not extend to the power to reject an application outright; that prerogative remains solely with the State Level Appraisal Committee. The applicant shall be notified in writing of any deficiencies identified during review, allowing for rectification prior to final assessment.

Applications for registration of industrial effluent treatment plants shall be submitted to the State Pollution Control Board in the prescribed format, along with a detailed project report outlining proposed construction methodologies and operational protocols. The Board may, after initial scrutiny, delegate the power to verify site suitability and assess compliance with environmental standards to authorized regional officers or committees constituted under this Act. Such delegation shall not relieve the Board of its ultimate responsibility for ensuring adherence to applicable regulations. Registration shall be granted subject to satisfactory completion of all prescribed inspections and submission of requisite documentation demonstrating financial viability and technical competence. The applicant shall provide proof of land ownership or leasehold rights, as deemed necessary by the Board.

Where a food business operator fails to pay any sum due from them under this Act or regulations made thereunder within thirty days of the date of demand served by the Food Safety Officer, the State Food Authority may issue an order for the recovery of such dues as arrears of land revenue. Such order shall specify the amount outstanding, including interest accrued at a rate determined by the Central Government, and detail the methods to be employed for recovery. Provided that, prior to issuing such an order, the food business operator shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate compliance or submit evidence contesting the assessed liability. The State Food Authority may also direct attachment of moveable property belonging to the defaulting food business operator, subject to due process as provided herein.

Where a food business operator fails to pay any sum due from them under this Act or regulations made thereunder within thirty days of the date of demand served by the Food Safety Officer, the State Food Authority may issue an order directing the recovery of the said amount as arrears of land revenue. Such order shall specify the amount outstanding, details of the default, and a further period of fifteen days for compliance. Provided that, before issuing such an order, the concerned food business operator shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate due diligence in attempting payment or provide evidence of circumstances preventing timely remittance. The recovery proceedings undertaken under this provision shall adhere strictly to procedures prescribed by applicable revenue laws, subject to any modifications deemed necessary by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, “licence” with regard to entities engaged in e-commerce activities means authorization granted by the Central Authority or designated agencies, subject to conditions specified therein. Such conditions shall relate to data security protocols, consumer grievance redressal mechanisms, and adherence to advertising guidelines as provided herein. A licence may be revoked if an entity fails to comply with these conditions, or engages in unfair trade practices detrimental to consumers. The Central Authority shall publish a register of all licences granted, including details of the specific conditions attached to each. Any modification to the conditions of a licence requires prior notification and opportunity for consumer representation.

Any person applying for a licence under this Act shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Licensing Authority designated by notification in the Official Gazette. The application shall include detailed particulars of the proposed arbitration facility, including its location, staffing levels, and anticipated caseload. Upon receipt of an application, the Licensing Authority may require the applicant to furnish further information or documentation deemed necessary for assessing suitability. The grant of a licence is subject to fulfilment of all conditions precedent as stipulated in Schedule A appended hereto. These conditions relate primarily to financial solvency, adherence to professional standards, and adequate provisions for data security. The Licensing Authority shall conduct an inspection prior to issuing a licence to verify compliance with these conditions. Any failure to meet the prescribed conditions may result in rejection of the application or imposition of remedial measures as determined by the Authority. Renewal of a licence is similarly conditional upon ongoing adherence to the requirements outlined herein.

The Central Licensing Authority may, upon application from a licensed food manufacturer intending to assign their manufacturing license, grant permission for said assignment subject to verification of the proposed assignee’s compliance with all applicable standards under this Act. Such an application shall detail the terms and conditions of the intended assignment, including but not limited to the duration of the existing license and any alterations to production processes planned by the assignee. The Authority may require a demonstration of financial stability from the prospective assignee prior to granting approval. Where a licensed food vendor fails to remit dues owed to a supplier under a contract related to the provision of ingredients or packaging materials, the supplier shall be entitled to initiate proceedings for recovery of those dues as provided herein. Any assignment undertaken without prior authorization from the Central Licensing Authority shall render the license liable for suspension.

Where a public authority fails to maintain records pertaining to decisions affecting the rights or liabilities of citizens, an aggrieved party may petition the appropriate appellate forum established under this Act. Such petitions shall be entertained if it is demonstrated that the absence of these records has demonstrably prejudiced the petitioner’s ability to pursue remedies available under law. The authority shall then direct the public body to undertake reasonable efforts to reconstruct such lost or destroyed records, provided that undue hardship or expense is not incurred in doing so. Failure by a public authority to comply with this direction may render its officers liable for damages as determined by the appellate forum. This provision applies irrespective of whether the destruction of records was intentional or accidental and operates without prejudice to any other right or remedy available to the petitioner under this Act.

Where a public authority fails to maintain records pertaining to decisions rendered or actions undertaken affecting the rights of citizens, such failure constitutes a denial of access to information and is actionable at law. Any citizen demonstrably prejudiced by the non-availability of relevant records may petition the appropriate adjudicating officer for redressal. The adjudicating officer shall direct the public authority to produce the missing records within a stipulated timeframe or, failing that, award compensation commensurate with the loss suffered by the petitioner. Such compensation shall include not only quantifiable financial detriment but also reasonable costs incurred in pursuing the remedy under this Act. Public authorities shall be deemed accountable for ensuring diligent maintenance of all official records; provided that inadvertent errors in record-keeping may be rectified without attracting penalty, subject to verification and correction procedures as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “licence” includes any authorisation granted under section 16, or otherwise as provided herein, permitting the generation, transmission, distribution, or supply of electricity; and "revocation" shall mean the withdrawal of such licence by the appropriate authority. The grounds for revocation include, but are not limited to, persistent failure to comply with safety regulations prescribed under this Act, demonstrable misrepresentation in any application for a licence, diversion of power intended for licensed distribution without due authorisation, or engaging in practices that create undue hardship to consumers. Subject to appeal as provided herein, a licence may be revoked if the licensee is found guilty of an offence involving corruption.

Registration of Consumer Grievance Redressal Forums shall be undertaken electronically through a centralized portal maintained by the Central Consumer Protection Authority. Each Forum established under this Act shall register all complaints received, assigning each a unique identification number for tracking purposes. Upon receipt of a complaint detailing alleged unfair trade practices or deficient services, the Registrar of the relevant Forum shall record particulars of the complainant, the respondent, and the nature of the grievance. Where the offence is compoundable as provided herein, an intimation regarding the possibility of compounding shall be prominently displayed on the registered complaint details within the portal. The Central Authority may prescribe guidelines for efficient registration and management of such compounded offences to ensure transparency in the process.

Revocation of contracts, as provided herein, is permitted where certain conditions are met; for the purposes of this Act, revocation signifies the communication of an intention to rescind a contract previously entered into, and shall only be effective when communicated to the other party in accordance with principles of reasonable notice. Grounds for such revocation include demonstrable misrepresentation forming the basis of consent, subsequent illegality rendering performance unlawful, or material alteration of contractual terms without prior agreement. Revocation is not permissible where the contract’s terms explicitly prohibit it, or where the act of revocation would be inequitable to the other party. The right to revoke shall be subject to any limitations prescribed under this Act.

Revocation of acceptance of an offer is deemed valid only when it is communicated to the proposer prior to the time the offeree undertakes performance at the request of the offeror or upon receiving notice of the dispatch of the acceptance. Such revocation operates as a rescission of the proposed contract, but shall not prejudice any right which the offeror may have under this Act. The grounds for revocation are limited to circumstances where the offeree reasonably believes that the offeror does not intend to perform, or where new information arises rendering performance impossible. Revocation is ineffective if the act in question constitutes a valid acceptance as provided herein.

Where a food business operator is charged with an offence relating to the manufacture, sale, or distribution of unsafe food, or misrepresentation regarding its contents, the prosecution shall bear the burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt every element of such offence. Provided that, where the alleged violation involves complex scientific analysis or testing procedures, the court may permit expert testimony to assist in determining the facts. The accused food business operator may present evidence rebutting the prosecution's case and demonstrating due diligence in adhering to prescribed standards under this Act. Failure to provide satisfactory proof of such due diligence shall not, however, absolve the accused from liability if the prosecution establishes the essential elements of the offence. Any consumer seeking redress for damages arising from consumption of unsafe food may also initiate proceedings as provided herein.

Where a food business operator is charged with an offence relating to the manufacture, sale, or distribution of unsafe food, the prosecution shall bear the burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt every element of the alleged offence. Provided that, where the food business operator alleges that the adulteration or misbranding occurred after the food came into their possession, the onus shall shift to such operator to demonstrate, by way of credible evidence, due diligence in handling and storage practices. Failure to provide such evidence does not preclude the prosecution from discharging its burden; it merely requires the operator to present a defence concerning the chain of custody. Any consumer seeking compensation for injury or loss resulting from unsafe food under this Act shall be entitled to recover damages as determined by the adjudicating officer, subject to the principles of natural justice and fair hearing.

Every Regional Transport Authority shall establish and maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all motor vehicles registered within its jurisdiction, including but not limited to details of ownership, registration dates, insurance coverage, fitness certificates, and emission compliance reports. These records shall be preserved securely and made accessible to authorized personnel for the purpose of administering this Act and enforcing its provisions. Any individual claiming damages arising from an accident involving a motor vehicle may request access to relevant records pertaining to that vehicle’s history, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Authority to protect privacy and prevent misuse. Failure to maintain accurate and complete records shall be deemed a violation under this Act, attracting penalties as determined by the Central Government. The Authority may prescribe guidelines for digitization of these records to ensure ease of access and data integrity.

Every Regional Transport Authority and every State Transport Undertaking shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to motor vehicles registered within their respective jurisdictions, including but not limited to details of registration, transfer of ownership, insurance policies, fitness certificates, and payment of taxes. These records shall be preserved for a minimum period of ten years from the date of the last transaction recorded therein. Any person claiming redress under this Act relating to vehicle registration or licensing may request certified copies of such records from the relevant authority, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Failure to provide accurate information or deliberate obfuscation within these maintained records shall constitute an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees and may render the responsible officer liable for further penalties as provided herein. The authority shall ensure that all data is accessible in a manner consistent with privacy regulations.

All registered consumer forums shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to every complaint filed, investigation undertaken, and order passed under this Act. These records shall include, but not be limited to, copies of all pleadings, evidence presented, interim orders issued, and final judgments rendered. The maintenance of such records is paramount for ensuring transparency and accountability within the redressal process. Consumer forums may utilize electronic means for record keeping, provided that adequate safeguards are implemented to prevent data loss or unauthorized access. All entries in physical registers shall be legible and permanently recorded. Records relating to complaints resolved through mediation shall be separately archived. Access to these records shall be subject to restrictions as prescribed by the Central Authority, ensuring privacy of complainants and respondents.

Every registered dealer engaged in providing goods or services subject to this Act shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all transactions undertaken during each financial year. These records must include, but are not limited to, invoices issued, receipts obtained, details of goods dispatched or services rendered, and a register of consumer complaints received and resolved. The maintenance of these records is crucial for ensuring transparency and accountability under this Act. Registered dealers shall preserve such records in an accessible format, either physical or electronic, for a period of not less than five years from the end of the financial year to which they relate. Failure to maintain adequate records as provided herein will be deemed a violation subject to penalties prescribed elsewhere.

For the purposes of this Act, a “limitation period” in relation to an arbitral proceeding or related legal proceedings shall mean the time within which a party is required to initiate action, whether for enforcement of an arbitral award or challenging the validity of an arbitration agreement or procedure. The limitation period applicable shall be determined by the law applied by the judicial authority seized of the matter, subject to any specific provisions under this Act prescribing shorter periods for particular claims. Where the relevant legislation does not specify a time limit, the court may determine a reasonable period considering principles of equity and fairness, provided that such determination does not prejudice the rights of either party.

For the purposes of this Act, a “limitation period” in relation to an arbitral proceeding or related legal proceedings shall mean the time within which a party is required to initiate action, whether for enforcing an arbitration agreement, challenging the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal, seeking enforcement of an arbitral award, or bringing any other claim arising from the arbitration. The limitation period shall be calculated from the date when the right to bring such action accrues, as determined under applicable principles of law and equity. Provided that where a party is prevented from initiating proceedings within the prescribed limitation period due to reasons beyond their control, the court may condone the delay subject to just cause being demonstrated.

The Central Food Safety Authority shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate its powers relating to inspection, sampling, and analysis of food articles to designated officers. Such delegation shall include the power to issue notices, seize adulterated or misbranded goods, and recommend prosecution for violations under this Act. An officer to whom powers are delegated shall exercise them in accordance with guidelines issued by the Central Food Safety Authority. The authority may revoke any such delegation at any time, provided that reasonable notice is given to the affected officer. No power vested in the Central Food Safety Authority can be delegated if it involves adjudication or determination of penalties exceeding a prescribed amount as defined herein.

The assignment of contractual obligations relating to broadcasting rights for sporting events shall be permitted subject to the conditions outlined herein. A licensor holding exclusive rights under this Act may delegate its powers pertaining to sub-licensing to a designated agent, provided that such delegation is documented through a written instrument executed by both parties and registered with the relevant authority. The licensee receiving such delegated power shall possess only those specific authorities expressly detailed within the assignment document; any actions exceeding these boundaries will be deemed ultra vires. Further, the original licensor retains ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with all terms stipulated under this Act. No transfer of rights shall prejudice existing obligations or liabilities incurred prior to the delegation. The assignee may not further delegate such powers without explicit written consent from the original licensor.

Where any food business operator is charged with contravention of regulations prescribed under this Act or with failing to comply with conditions stipulated in a license issued thereunder, the onus of establishing innocence shall lie upon that operator. The adjudicating officer may require the operator to produce documentary evidence and witness testimony demonstrating adherence to applicable standards. Any such determination made by the adjudicating officer is subject to appeal before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal. Provided that the appellate tribunal shall not substitute its own findings for those of the adjudicating officer unless it finds, on a preponderance of the evidence presented, that the original decision was manifestly arbitrary or based on an erroneous interpretation of the law as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "revocation" with regard to contracts for supply of goods or services includes the termination of such contract by the consumer due to demonstrable failure on the part of the service provider. Such revocation shall be permissible where the service provided is substantially deficient in quality, deviates significantly from advertised specifications, or constitutes an unfair trade practice as defined under this Act. The right to revoke a contract does not extend to services wholly consumed prior to discovery of the deficiency, subject to any regulations prescribed by the Central Government. Revocation shall operate as if the contract was never entered into, entitling the consumer to full refund of consideration paid, provided that such claim is made within three years from the date of agreement.

The Public Authority shall maintain all records deemed relevant to the exercise of its functions as provided herein, ensuring accessibility for citizens seeking information under this Act. Such maintenance includes, but is not limited to, digitization of documents where feasible and preservation of physical records according to established archival protocols. Any third party holding dominion over records generated by a Public Authority may, with prior written consent from the Information Commission, license access or assign rights relating to those records for commercial purposes; provided that such licensing or assignment explicitly safeguards the privacy of individuals and complies with all applicable provisions concerning data security. The Public Authority shall retain ultimate responsibility for ensuring accuracy and completeness of information contained within any licensed or assigned record set. Further, under this Act, any transfer of maintenance responsibilities must be documented and reported to the Central Information Commission.

Where an arbitral award has been made, a party seeking revocation thereof may apply to the designated judicial authority alleging that the award was induced by fraud or misrepresentation; such application shall be accompanied by supporting evidence demonstrating the material nature of the deception and its direct bearing on the outcome of the arbitration. The judicial authority shall consider whether the alleged conduct rendered the arbitral process fundamentally unfair, precluding a just resolution of the dispute. Grounds for revocation are strictly limited to instances of demonstrable fraud or misrepresentation as provided herein; allegations of bias or error in law do not constitute valid grounds under this Act. Any order revoking an award shall be subject to review on appeal by the appellate authority, and costs associated with such proceedings shall be determined according to prevailing rules.

Where an offence involving property has been committed, and the offender offers to restore the property taken or damaged to its original condition, or compensate the injured person for the loss sustained, the Court may, subject to any directions issued by the State Government, permit the compounding of the offence under this Act. Such permission shall be deemed a license granted solely for the purpose of facilitating restitution and does not constitute an acquittal nor prejudice any other proceedings against the offender. The right to grant such permission remains exclusively with the Court, and no assignment or transfer of this licensing authority may occur between Courts or judicial officers. Further, any agreement entered into concerning the compounding shall be recorded in writing and filed with the Court; failure to adhere to its terms will render the agreement void ab initio.

Where any offence involving pecuniary loss to a person has been committed, and the offender offers to compensate the injured party for the said loss, and the offer is accepted by that party, the Court may, subject to provisions of this Act and other applicable laws, permit the compounding of the offence in such manner as it deems fit. Such permission shall not preclude the Court from considering any aggravating factors relating to the commission of the offence or the conduct of the offender. Any agreement for compensation entered into under this provision shall be recorded by the Court and form part of the judgment. The right to compound an offence, as provided herein, is assignable only with the express written consent of the injured party, which consent must also be recorded by the Court.

Any person found to have engaged in fraudulent activities relating to arbitration proceedings, including but not limited to fabrication of evidence or collusion with arbitrators, shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be subject to a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, such individual’s assets derived from the aforementioned fraudulent conduct are deemed forfeit to the State. Where an offence under this Act is compounded as provided herein, the compounding officer may require the offender to pay compensation to any party aggrieved by the said offence, the amount determined based on demonstrable losses incurred. Failure to comply with a compounding order shall render the individual subject to prosecution under this Act and applicable penal code provisions.

Where an arbitral award has been made in terms of a settlement agreement, and one party subsequently alleges material misrepresentation or fraud induced by the other party during the negotiation of said settlement, that party may apply to the designated judicial authority for revocation of the award under this Act. Such application shall be accompanied by supporting affidavits detailing the circumstances giving rise to the alleged misrepresentation or fraud, and demonstrating a causal link between such deception and the acceptance of the terms embodied in the arbitral award. The judicial authority shall afford both parties an opportunity to present evidence and argument; provided that the burden of proving fraud lies solely upon the applicant. Any order revoking an award under these provisions is subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Every licensed food vendor undertaking operations involving manufacturing, processing, packaging, storage, distribution, catering, or import of any article of food shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all stages of these activities. These records must include particulars relating to raw materials received, ingredients used, processes employed, personnel involved in handling food, and the destination of finished products. The Authority may prescribe the form and manner in which such records are maintained, including electronic formats subject to verification protocols. Assignment of a license under this Act shall not absolve the assignor from responsibility for ensuring continued compliance with record-keeping requirements until the expiry or revocation of the assignment. Failure to maintain adequate records as provided herein constitutes an offence punishable under this Act and may render the license liable for suspension.

Every license holder engaged in the manufacture, processing, packing, storage, distribution, or sale of food products shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all activities undertaken under this Act. These records must include, but are not limited to, raw material procurement details, batch production numbers, quality control testing results, employee training logs, and pest control measures implemented. Assignment of a license to another party shall require the transfer of all existing records relating to food safety compliance to the assignee, as certified by the licensing authority. Failure to provide complete and accurate records, or any attempt to conceal information, will render the licensee liable for penalties under this Act. The Food Safety Officer may at any time inspect these records; provided that such inspections shall be conducted in a manner consistent with principles of natural justice.

For the purposes of this Act, “limitation period” means the time within which a consumer must institute proceedings against an entity for redressal of grievances arising from deficient goods or services, or unfair trade practices. The limitation period shall generally be two years from the date on which the cause of action arose. Provided that in cases involving claims relating to financial services, the limitation period may extend to three years from the relevant date as determined by regulations framed under this Act. This period is subject to potential extension where fraud, misrepresentation, or concealment of material facts are alleged. The Central Authority may issue guidelines concerning the calculation and application of the limitation period.

For the purposes of this Act, “limitation period” in relation to any claim arising from a deficiency in goods or services shall mean the maximum time within which a consumer has recourse to file a complaint before the relevant adjudicating authority or consumer forum. This limitation period shall be three years commencing from the date on which the cause of action arose; provided that, where the deficiency involves fraud, misrepresentation, or concealment, the limitation period may be extended by a further two years at the discretion of the adjudicating authority. The commencement of proceedings under this Act is subject to just and equitable considerations as determined by the forum.

Where a consumer has obtained relief under this Act through an order passed by a District Commission, State Commission or National Commission, that order may be revoked if it is subsequently determined that the proceedings were conducted in violation of natural justice; provided that such determination shall only be made where the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the alleged procedural irregularity. The revocation of an order shall not be permissible unless the concerned regulatory body establishes, beyond reasonable doubt, that the consumer was afforded no opportunity to present their case or rebut evidence presented against them. Further, any appeal against a revocation order may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of such order and subject to conditions as provided herein.

Where a consumer has obtained relief under this Act through an order passed by a District Commission, State Commission or National Commission, that order may be revoked if it is subsequently determined that the proceedings were conducted in violation of principles of natural justice. Such revocation shall only occur where the aggrieved party demonstrates to the appropriate forum, as provided herein, that they were not afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their case and rebut evidence offered by the opposite party. Further, revocation is permissible if material information was withheld from either party which would have substantially altered the outcome. The Commission may also order revocation if it finds that the relief granted was induced by fraud or misrepresentation on the part of the consumer. This power of revocation shall be exercised sparingly and subject to a finding of demonstrable prejudice.

Where an offence involving personal injury or loss of property is compounded between the offender and the injured party, subject to the provisions of Chapter IX of this Act relating to civil procedure, any agreement made in that regard shall be void and incapable of affecting the rights of any other person claiming redress for the same offence. Provided that, if it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Court that such compounding was effected without coercion or undue influence upon either party, and with full understanding of the consequences under this Act and relevant penal laws, the Court may, at its discretion, consider the agreement as a mitigating factor during sentencing. Any appeal against an order refusing recognition of a valid compoundable offence shall lie to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where a party is required or permitted under this Act to serve notice or other communication upon another party, such service shall be effected by registered post with acknowledgment due, or by courier, or by electronic means where the recipient has consented in writing to accept service in that manner. Provided that, if the address of the addressee is not known, service may be accomplished by publication in a widely circulated newspaper circulating within the jurisdiction where the arbitration agreement was entered into. The party effecting service shall provide evidence of dispatch and receipt, or attempted receipt, as applicable, and failure to obtain acknowledgment under registered post shall not preclude enforcement of the communication. Any such electronic transmission must comply with security protocols prescribed by regulations framed in accordance with this Act.

Where a party is required or permitted under this Act to serve notice or other document upon another party, such service shall be effected by registered post acknowledgement due or by courier service or by email, provided that the address for service of any party is as notified in writing prior to the institution of arbitration proceedings. Where service by registered post is elected, it shall be deemed to have been duly served on the date appearing on the postal receipt; where service by courier is effected, it shall be deemed to have been duly served when delivery is acknowledged by the recipient or their authorized representative; and where service is by email, it shall be deemed complete upon transmission, subject to confirmation of receipt. The party effecting service shall retain proof of dispatch and, if applicable, acknowledgement of receipt as evidence thereof.

All persons engaged in activities listed under Schedule I, or any subsequent activity approved under this Act, shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to environmental impact assessments, pollution control measures implemented, and waste management protocols adopted at their respective sites. These records must be preserved for a minimum period of ten years from the date of cessation of operations and shall be accessible for inspection by authorized officers appointed under this Act upon reasonable notice. The format and content of such records shall adhere to guidelines issued by the Central Pollution Control Board, as amended from time to time. Failure to maintain adequate records or obstructing access thereto will attract penalties as provided herein. Every record created pursuant to these provisions constitutes official documentation subject to verification and audit.

All persons engaged in activities listed under Schedule I, including but not limited to industries generating hazardous waste or operating thermal power plants, shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to environmental impact assessments, pollution control measures implemented, and quantities of pollutants discharged. These records must be preserved for a minimum period of ten years from the date of commencement of operations and made available for inspection by authorized officers upon request. The Central Pollution Control Board may prescribe standard formats for these records to ensure uniformity in data collection. Failure to maintain such records or providing false information therein shall be deemed an offence under this Act, punishable with monetary penalties as provided herein. Every record created pursuant to this provision becomes public document accessible subject to reasonable restrictions.

Where a generating company is granted a licence under this Act, the conditions of that licence shall be binding on the licensee and subject to review by the State Commission upon application by any distribution licensee or consumer group demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from those conditions. Provided that, any such application for review must specify with particularity the alleged detrimental effect and provide supporting data verifiable through independent audit. The Commission may, after affording the generating company a reasonable opportunity of being heard, modify the licence conditions as it deems just and equitable; however, such modification shall not prejudice existing contractual obligations entered into in good faith prior to the application. Any party aggrieved by an order of the State Commission under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, “offence” with regard to failure to pay gratuity includes any act or omission constituting a violation of duty imposed upon an employer under this Act or any rule made thereunder. The term "employer" shall include any establishment as defined herein and every person legally entitled to receive gratuity. An offence specified in this Act may be compounded, subject to such terms and conditions as the Controlling Authority deems fit, provided that the compounding amount is deposited with the authority within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of notice issued under this Act. The power to compound an offence shall vest solely with the Controlling Authority.

Every business engaged in providing goods or services shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to consumer transactions, including but not limited to purchase details, service agreements, warranty information, and complaint resolutions. These records must be preserved securely for a minimum period of five years from the date of the transaction, and shall be accessible for inspection by authorized officers under this Act during business hours. Failure to adequately maintain such records will constitute an unfair trade practice, rendering the business liable for penalties as provided herein. Consumers are entitled to request copies of their relevant transactional data held by businesses, subject to reasonable fees determined by regulations framed in accordance with this Act. The Central Authority may issue guidelines regarding digitization and secure storage of these records to ensure efficient retrieval and consumer access.

Where a distribution licensee fails to provide electricity service in the manner prescribed under this Act or regulations made thereunder, any consumer affected thereby may file a complaint with the Grievance Redressal Forum established by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. The Forum shall afford both the complainant and the licensee an opportunity for argument and presentation of evidence relating to the alleged deficiency in service. Provided that the licensee may submit documentary proof demonstrating adherence to prescribed standards, which shall be considered by the Forum. Any order made by the Grievance Redressal Forum is appealable to the State Commission within thirty days from the date of such order; subject to the satisfaction of the Commission regarding the maintainability of the appeal.

The Central Pollution Control Board may, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate its powers and functions relating to the inspection of industrial premises and the assessment of environmental impact statements to officers appointed by it specifically for that purpose, provided that such delegation shall only occur after prior consultation with the concerned State Pollution Control Board. Any officer so delegated shall be required to submit a monthly report detailing all inspections conducted and findings made, to both the Central Pollution Control Board and the relevant State Pollution Control Board. The Central Government may issue guidelines specifying the qualifications and experience necessary for officers eligible for such delegation. Further, any decision taken by an officer acting under delegated authority is subject to review by the Central Pollution Control Board upon request from any affected party.

The Central Pollution Control Board may, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate its powers and duties relating to inspection, monitoring, and assessment of compliance with environmental standards to authorized officers or committees constituted for specific purposes; provided that any such delegation shall be accompanied by a written instrument clearly defining the scope and limitations of the delegated authority. Such delegations shall only be made where the Board is reasonably satisfied that the delegate possesses the requisite technical expertise and impartiality to perform the assigned functions effectively. Further, no power relating to the imposition of penalties or remedial measures under this Act may be delegated; all such actions remain exclusively within the purview of the Central Pollution Control Board or its designated officers acting under direct instruction.

The Regional Transport Authority shall have power to delegate its functions relating to the issuance of permits for commercial vehicles, including specialized transport carriers, to authorized licensing officers appointed under this Act. Such delegation may include authority regarding the assignment of existing vehicle permits upon sale or transfer of ownership, subject to adherence with prescribed conditions and verification procedures. The Licensing Officer so delegated shall be empowered to approve assignments only where the transferee meets all eligibility criteria as stipulated under this Act and provides satisfactory proof of financial stability and operational capacity. Any such assignment requires prior notification to the Regional Transport Authority and may be rejected if deemed detrimental to public transport interests or in violation of any existing regulations. The authority retains ultimate oversight, and may revoke delegated powers at any time, provided that reasonable notice is given.

The Regional Transport Authority, while exercising powers vested under this Act relating to the issuance of permits for commercial vehicles, may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate specific functions pertaining to the verification of vehicle documents and assessment of fitness certificates to authorized Vehicle Inspection Officers. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a detailed schedule outlining the scope and limitations of the delegated authority, including monetary thresholds beyond which decisions must be referred back to the RTA for review. The Authority may also authorize recognized transport associations to submit applications on behalf of permit applicants, subject to an indemnity bond guaranteeing accuracy of information provided. Any assignment of responsibility under this delegation requires prior written consent from the RTA and shall remain valid only as long as the Vehicle Inspection Officer or association maintains accreditation, as determined by a periodic assessment process.

The Central Authority established under this Act may, through notification published in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers to any officer of the level of Deputy Director or higher, for purposes relating to the grant, modification, or revocation of licenses issued pursuant to regulations framed under this Act. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a clear specification of the delegated authority’s scope and limitations. Any licensee desiring to assign their rights and obligations pertaining to a license granted under this Act shall obtain prior written consent from the Central Authority, provided that such assignment does not result in a change of control exceeding twenty-six percent ownership. The Central Authority may impose conditions on any such assignment deemed necessary to protect consumer interests as provided herein. This power of delegation extends only to administrative functions and does not include the authority to adjudicate disputes under this Act.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority may, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, delegate its powers and functions relating to the investigation, inquiry, and settlement of consumer disputes arising from unfair trade practices to a designated officer or committee appointed by the Authority. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a written instrument specifying the scope and duration of the delegated authority, and may include the power to issue notices, conduct hearings, and impose penalties as provided herein. No such delegation shall extend to the power to initiate investigations concerning systemic failures affecting multiple consumers unless specifically authorized by resolution passed by the Authority’s governing body. Assignment of responsibilities relating to consumer redressal mechanisms established under this Act requires prior written consent from the affected consumer, ensuring transparency in the process and safeguarding individual rights as contemplated herein.

Every consumer dispute resolution agency shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all complaints received, investigations undertaken, orders passed, and recoveries effected under this Act. Such records shall include, but not be limited to, copies of written complaints, correspondence with parties involved, assessment reports, reasoned orders, and documentation relating to the disbursement of funds or compensation awarded. The licensing of access to these records for commercial data processing purposes may be granted by the Central Authority, subject to stringent conditions safeguarding consumer privacy and confidentiality. Any assignment of rights pertaining to such licensed data shall require prior written consent from the Central Authority and will remain valid only as long as the original license is in effect. Failure to maintain adequate records or unauthorized assignment thereof shall constitute an offence punishable under this Act.

Every consumer dispute resolution agency shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all complaints received, investigations undertaken, orders passed, and penalties imposed under this Act. Such records shall include, but not be limited to, copies of written complaints, correspondence with parties involved, findings of fact, reasoning for decisions, and details of any compensation awarded. The authority may authorize a third party to maintain these records electronically, subject to stringent data security protocols as prescribed by regulations framed in consultation with the Central Consumer Protection Authority. Any assignment or licensing of the right to access or process such maintained records shall require prior written consent from the relevant consumer dispute resolution agency and be governed by conditions ensuring confidentiality and adherence to applicable law. The maintenance of these records is crucial for transparency and accountability under this Act.

Every distribution licensee shall maintain detailed records pertaining to electricity supply, including but not limited to meter readings, consumption data, billing information, and complaint resolutions, in a manner accessible for inspection by authorized officers under this Act. Failure to do so shall be deemed a violation subject to penalty as prescribed herein. Any consumer disputing the accuracy of any record maintained by the licensee may file a written objection with the designated grievance redressal forum, accompanied by supporting documentation. The licensee shall investigate such objections expeditiously and provide a reasoned response in writing within thirty days. Decisions of the grievance redressal forum are appealable to the State Commission, provided that appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of the order appealed against.

Every distribution licensee shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to electricity supply, including but not limited to metering data, consumer complaints received, outages experienced, and payments collected, in a manner accessible for inspection by authorized officers under this Act. The precise format and duration of record retention shall be prescribed by regulations framed by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission; provided that any dispute arising regarding the accuracy or completeness of such records may be referred to an independent auditor appointed by the Commission. Failure to maintain adequate records, or demonstrable negligence in their preservation, shall constitute a violation subject to penalties as determined under this Act. Any party contesting the validity of charges levied based on disputed record entries may appeal to the appellate tribunal within sixty days.

Every occupier of an industrial establishment generating waste hazardous to the environment shall maintain detailed records pertaining to the nature, quantity, and disposal methods employed for all such wastes. These records shall include, but are not limited to, manifests documenting transfer of waste, analytical reports verifying composition, and inventories detailing storage locations. The State Pollution Control Board may prescribe a standard format for these records, which shall be adhered to strictly. Failure to maintain adequate records as provided herein constitutes an offence under this Act and is subject to penalties as determined by the Board. Records are to be preserved for a period of not less than five years from the date of generation of the waste. Any person found obstructing access to such records by authorized officers of the Board shall be deemed guilty of contravention.

Where a principal has delegated authority to an agent for the performance of a contract, such delegation shall only be valid if it is expressly or impliedly authorized under this Act. The power to delegate shall not extend beyond the scope of the agency originally conferred upon the agent, and any act performed by a sub-agent acting outside that defined scope shall render the principal liable as though the original agent had acted directly. Provided that, where the nature of the contract requires personal skill or competence of the agent, delegation is prohibited unless the principal has explicitly waived this requirement in writing. The principal remains responsible for ensuring compliance with all applicable laws and regulations pertaining to the contractual obligations, even if delegated. Any deviation from agreed terms by a sub-agent shall be deemed an act attributable to the original agent.

Where a principal has delegated authority to an agent under this Act for the performance of specific contractual obligations, such delegation shall not relieve the principal from ultimate responsibility unless expressly agreed upon in writing with all parties involved. The agent shall exercise the delegated powers diligently and in accordance with instructions received from the principal, provided that any deviation from these instructions requires prior written consent from the principal. Failure by the agent to comply with reasonable directions of the principal shall render the delegation ineffective against third parties. Where the nature of the contractual obligation necessitates personal performance by the principal, such obligations are not susceptible to delegation as provided herein. The principal may revoke the delegated authority at any time, subject to equitable considerations concerning reliance by third parties.

Every distribution licensee holding a licence under this Act shall remain liable to have that licence revoked if it is found that they persistently fail to adhere to prescribed standards of service quality as determined by the State Commission. Such failure includes, but is not limited to, repeated instances of unauthorized disconnections without due process and demonstrable negligence in responding to consumer complaints regarding power outages. The revocation may also be ordered where a licensee engages in practices detrimental to the efficient operation of the grid, or obstructs investigations undertaken under this Act by authorized officers. Any person aggrieved by an order for revocation may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days; however, such appeal shall not suspend the effect of the revocation until its determination. Failure to comply with a revocation order constitutes an offence punishable with a fine.

Where a person is accused of an offence relatable to the improper use of a motor vehicle or a breach of a condition thereof, the Transport Officer concerned shall, upon receiving information regarding the alleged offence, issue a notice to the offender requiring his appearance before such officer at a specified time and place. The offender shall be afforded an opportunity to present his case and produce evidence in mitigation. Following this hearing, if the Transport Officer considers it appropriate, he may direct that the said offence be compounded under this Act. Such compounding shall involve the payment of a sum determined by the Transport Officer, which shall not exceed [amount] for offences specified in Schedule A and [amount] for those detailed in Schedule B. The amount so paid shall be remitted to the State Road Fund. Provided that no compounding shall be ordered where the offence involves serious injury or death.

Any officer authorized by the Central Government under this Act may, subject to conditions specified in the notification granting authorization, delegate any of their powers relating to inspection, investigation, or enforcement to other officers subordinate to them. Such delegation shall not extend to the power to impose penalties exceeding fifty thousand rupees, nor to the initiation of prosecution proceedings. Any person found to be obstructing an authorized officer exercising delegated powers shall be liable to a penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term not less than six months. Failure to comply with directions issued by an officer acting under delegated authority constitutes an offence punishable with a fine, as provided herein.

Any officer authorized under this Act to exercise powers relating to environmental protection may, subject to general directions from the Central Government, delegate those powers to other officers subordinate to him or her. Such delegation shall specify the particular functions and geographical areas to which it applies. Any person failing to comply with an order issued by a delegated authority shall be liable to pay a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term extending up to six months, as determined by the adjudicating officer. Repeated or willful non-compliance will attract enhanced penalties, including suspension of operations causing environmental harm, provided that the original authorizing officer retains ultimate responsibility for actions taken under delegated powers.

The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission may, through notification published in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers relating to the grant of licenses for electricity trading to a designated authority constituted under this Act. Such delegation shall include the power to consider applications for license modification concerning assignment of existing trading licenses and to determine the terms and conditions governing such assignments. The delegated authority shall exercise these powers subject to guidelines issued by the Commission, which may specify limitations on the scope of assignable rights including but not limited to transmission infrastructure access agreements and contractual obligations entered into prior to assignment. Provided that any assignment undertaken in violation of these guidelines shall be deemed invalid, and the original licensee remains liable for all outstanding obligations. The Commission may revoke such delegation at any time after giving one month’s notice.

The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission may, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate its powers relating to the grant, renewal, modification, or cancellation of licenses for the transmission of electricity to a designated authority constituted under this section. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a formal order specifying the extent and duration of the delegated power, and detailing any conditions applicable thereto. Any license granted pursuant to such delegation shall be deemed to have been granted by the Commission itself. The assignment of rights associated with a transmission license, including but not limited to those pertaining to infrastructure assets or contractual obligations, requires prior written consent from the Commission. This consent may be withheld if the proposed assignee does not meet the financial and technical criteria as provided herein.

Where any offence relatable to the Motor Vehicles Act has been committed, the officer authorised under this Act may, subject to conditions specified herein, compound the offence with the offender by accepting from him such sum as may be prescribed. Provided that no compounding shall take place if a police report has been filed in respect of the offence or if the offence involves injury to any person. Any party aggrieved by an order made relating to the compounding of an offence under this Act may, within thirty days from the date of such order, file an appeal before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal exercising jurisdiction over the area where the offence was committed; and the Tribunal shall consider all relevant materials on record and pass a reasoned order.

Where any offence relatable to the Motor Vehicles Act has been committed, and where the offender admits guilt and makes full restitution to the victim or their nominee, the concerned Transport Authority may, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, entertain a request for compounding of the said offence. Provided that such compounding shall only be permissible in cases involving minor traffic violations as determined by notification issued by the State Government from time to time. Any party aggrieved by an order directing or refusing compounding may within thirty days of such order file an appeal before the Regional Transport Appellate Authority, and the appellate authority shall consider any relevant evidence presented and pass a reasoned order.

For the purposes of this Act, revocation is defined as the rescission or annulment of a prior act, agreement, or disposition. Grounds for revocation include subsequent fraud, misrepresentation, coercion, or undue influence affecting the volition of the party revoking. A gift may be revoked if it was made in contemplation of marriage and such marriage does not take place. Similarly, a will is subject to revocation based on demonstrable material alteration after its execution. The power to revoke shall vest solely in the person who initially performed the act or their legally appointed representative, provided that the right to revocation is extinguished by effluxion of time as may be prescribed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, revocation is defined as the rescission or annulment of a previous act, agreement, or disposition. Grounds for revocation include, but are not limited to, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake, coercion, and undue influence. An offeror may revoke an offer at any time prior to acceptance by the offeree, subject to exceptions provided herein regarding firm offers and options contracts. A party shall be deemed to have revoked a contract where such party communicates an unequivocal intention to abandon it. Revocation operates as of the point when communication is received or, in cases of conduct, when the act constituting revocation becomes apparent.

The Central Pollution Control Board may, with prior approval of the Ministry, delegate its powers under this Act relating to the inspection of industrial premises and the issuance of directions concerning environmental safeguards to any officer in the regular time scale of its service; provided that such delegation shall be accompanied by a written instrument specifying the precise extent and limitations of the delegated authority. Any order passed by an officer acting under such delegated power shall be deemed to have been passed by the Central Pollution Control Board itself, and is subject to challenge before the National Green Tribunal on grounds of manifest error or exceeding the scope of the delegation. The aggrieved party may appeal any decision rendered by the Tribunal within sixty days, as provided herein, to the Supreme Court.

The Central Pollution Control Board shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have power to delegate its functions relating to the inspection of industrial premises and the assessment of environmental impact statements to officers appointed by the Board or to recognized agencies. Such delegation shall be deemed to be valid only if accompanied by a written instrument specifying the precise scope and limitations of the delegated authority, which instrument is subject to review and revocation at any time. Any order passed by an officer acting under such delegated power may be challenged before the Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of its communication, and the Authority shall consider whether the delegation was lawfully effected and if so, whether the exercise of that power was reasonable and in accordance with principles of natural justice.

Where a party has unequivocally communicated his intention to revoke a contract to the other party, the revocation shall be deemed complete upon receipt of that communication, or where transmission is by post, upon misdirection or delay beyond reasonable limits attributable to postal services. Any notice purporting to be such revocation must be in writing and delivered personally or sent by registered post with acknowledgement due. The recipient of a purported revocation may challenge its validity before the District Magistrate within thirty days from the date of receipt, submitting evidence demonstrating that the communication did not constitute an unequivocal intention to revoke as provided herein. Failure to submit such a challenge within the stipulated period shall be conclusive proof of revocation’s efficacy. The onus of proving unequivocal intent rests upon the party claiming revocation. This provision shall apply irrespective of any prior agreements concerning contract termination procedures.
